Sela revealed that the clinic offered treatment in exchange for household citizenship credits, occupational guarantees, or removal of a dependent from the household register; she has not yet agreed to transfer credits.
Master Orin Vale warned Mara that the cartography archives beneath the office contain discarded knowledge and explicitly cautioned her to stay away from them.
Mara will consider entering the sealed archive beneath the Office of Cartography to search obsolete medical and infrastructure records for a treatment or explanation for Eli’s denial.
Sela will face the imminent choice of transferring or selling household citizenship credits, risking housing, power allocation, and Mara’s certification, to obtain Eli’s treatment.

chapters.name: The Sealed Archive
chapters.content:
That night, Mara waited until the apartment had gone quiet enough to hear the concentrator working.

Eli’s breath came in uneven pulls through the tube. Sela slept in her clothes on the narrow couch, one hand curled around the black transfer key. The citizenship ledger lay beneath her elbow, its corners pressing into the fabric of her jacket. Mara stood in the kitchen doorway and watched them both, feeling the weight of the promise she had made: another way, something useful.

There was no useful way left inside the rules.

She dressed in her maintenance coveralls, dark gray rather than the pale blue of cartography apprentices. The coveralls belonged to Sela and hung loose at the shoulders, but a utility worker’s tag would open doors that an apprentice tag could not. Mara had copied the tag’s emergency credentials months ago while updating the filtration-access map. She had told herself it was ordinary professional caution. Now the copied code sat in a temporary credential on her tablet, bright and incriminating.

Before leaving, she knelt beside Eli’s alcove.

His eyes opened. “You’re very bad at sneaking.”

Mara froze. “Go back to sleep.”

“Where are you going?”

“Work.”

“At midnight?”

“Cartography never sleeps.”

“Cartography should see a doctor.”

His smile faded when she did not smile back. The concentrator clicked and changed pitch. “Don’t get caught,” he whispered.

“I won’t.”

“That’s another dangerous promise.”

“I know.”

She touched his forehead, then left before he could ask for the truth.

The city after hours was not empty. Lumen never became empty. Even when the public lifts stopped singing their arrival chimes, pumps labored behind walls, service vehicles moved along narrow maintenance tracks, and the buoyancy engines beat beneath the floors with a force Mara felt in her teeth. In the lower rings, workers traveled between shifts under amber emergency lighting. Their faces appeared and vanished in doorways, anonymous as figures on a map.

Mara took a service lift from Ring Twelve to the Office of Cartography. Her borrowed tag opened the first gate. At the second, the reader paused long enough for sweat to gather beneath her collar.

AUTHORIZED EMERGENCY ACCESS, the screen decided.

The gate released with a sigh.

The office was dark except for the blue standby lights of the drafting stations. Orin’s maps hung in the corridor like pale windows. Mara walked past the old coastline of southern England without looking at it. She had memorized the stairwell door during the day, including the places where its paint had bubbled and where the lower hinge had been repaired with a strip of mismatched metal.

Her tablet displayed the access schematic. The official stairwell ended at Level One. The old route continued downward through a maintenance shaft, then branched toward the archive stacks. Most of the lines were gray. One pulsed yellow.

T-17.

The designation appeared again, not as a corridor but as an emergency transfer route. Mara stared at it. It might have been a coincidence. It might have been an old naming convention. Or it might be the same hidden route whose coordinates she had copied months ago from an external observation notation.

She saved a second copy and began descending.

The first flight smelled of dust and hot wiring. The second smelled of metal wet with condensation. At the bottom, a pressure door blocked the stairs. Mara pressed Sela’s copied credential to the reader.

The door remained shut.

She tried the emergency code manually. The screen asked for a work order, a supervisor authorization, and a reason for entry. She selected MEMBRANE FAILURE, then typed a string of numbers from the lower-ring ventilation grid. The system thought for several seconds.

A red camera lens turned toward her.

Mara kept her face blank. “Filter pressure variance,” she said, though no one was listening.

The lock released.

Beyond it, the archive level had been built in a different age. The walls were concrete instead of composite, and the ceiling was low enough that Mara had to duck beneath old cable trays. A line of faded lettering ran along one wall: CARTOGRAPHIC STORAGE—PRE-CONTINUANCE / ACCESS BY ORDER.

Someone had painted over the final words. The gray coating had cracked, exposing the phrase beneath like a bone.

Mara switched on her wrist lamp.

Shelves stretched into darkness. Polymer cases leaned at angles where the floor had shifted. Some had swollen from damp and split open, spilling sheets of translucent survey film across the concrete. A dead cleaning drone rested on its side beside a drainage grate, one articulated arm still extended toward a smear of black mold.

She had expected records to be arranged in some recognizable order. Instead, the archive seemed to have been abandoned during an argument. Crates were labeled with dates but stacked according to no date she could see. Medical data occupied one aisle, then disappeared behind a collapsed rack. Infrastructure plans were mixed with agricultural surveys and emergency evacuation notices.

Mara set the tablet on a crate and searched the index terminal.

The terminal woke reluctantly. Its display filled with static, then a list of categories.

RESPIRATORY CONDITIONS.
EARLY ATMOSPHERIC EXPOSURE.
LUMENEX PRECURSORS.
DEPENDENT CARE ALLOCATIONS.

Her heart struck hard against her ribs.

She selected LUMENEX PRECURSORS.

ACCESS DENIED—CLASSIFICATION OBSOLETE.

“Obsolete doesn’t mean useless,” she said.

The terminal offered no response. She tried an alternate query using Eli’s condition, then the original medical code from his clinic file. The system returned three entries, all marked transferred. She followed the transfer references to a storage aisle and found two empty cases. The third had been sealed with a brittle red strip.

Inside were not treatment instructions but old atmospheric exposure studies. The pages described children who had developed damaged lungs during the years before Lumen’s stabilizers were completed. Several notes mentioned an inhaled compound that reduced inflammation. The dosage tables were incomplete, but the chemical family was close enough to Lumenex that Mara copied every visible line.

A warning appeared on the tablet: SOURCE INTEGRITY UNVERIFIED.

She ignored it.

A metallic clank echoed from deeper in the archive.

Mara killed her lamp and crouched behind the case.

The sound did not repeat. Water ticked somewhere in the ceiling. The archive settled around her with slow, hidden movements. She waited until her pulse calmed, then turned the lamp back on.

The nearest terminal had changed screens.

A system notice glowed in white letters:

UNSCHEDULED ACCESS RECORDED.
SECURITY REVIEW IN PROGRESS.

Mara’s stomach tightened. She reached for the tablet and began copying the files faster. The old terminal’s transfer port accepted the connection, but each record moved slowly, a thin bar crawling across the screen. She copied the exposure studies, the incomplete dosage table, and a list of experimental compounds. Then she copied the access log showing that the files had been sealed six years after the Continuance.

A red icon appeared at the edge of the display.

REMOTE OBSERVER ACTIVE.

She pulled the cable free.

The archive lights flickered on.

Not all of them. A row of lamps came alive far down the central aisle, then another row, illuminating the shelves one section at a time. The automated security system was not using the cameras alone. It was searching the room by light.

Mara slipped the tablet beneath her coveralls and moved.

She had mapped the archive entrance. She had not mapped the archive itself. The aisles bent around support columns, and several shelves had fallen across the marked route. She climbed over one, caught her boot on a loose cable, and nearly fell into a shallow trench where old data conduits had been exposed.

A soft chime sounded behind her.

ACCESS SUBJECT LOCATED.

She ran.

The medical aisle ended at a sealed partition. Mara threw herself sideways into a narrow gap between two racks as a security drone floated around the corner. It was no larger than a suitcase, with a black camera dome and two retractable arms. Its search beam swept across the floor.

She held her breath.

The drone paused beside the rack. One arm unfolded, its tip glowing blue. Mara saw the reflection in a puddle before she saw the device itself. The scanner was reading heat and movement.

Her hand found a loose data wafer on the floor.

She tossed it down the opposite aisle.

The wafer struck a pipe. The drone pivoted and glided after the sound. Mara slid through the gap, pressed against the partition, and searched for a latch. Her fingers found a recessed panel. She entered the same ventilation-grid numbers she had used at the door.

The panel opened.

She squeezed through just as the drone’s blue beam swept over the place where she had been.

On the other side, the air was colder. The room beyond held no shelves, only a circular table and a wall-sized display filmed with dust. The display woke when she approached.

A map appeared.

At first Mara thought it was a rendering of Lumen’s approved history: the drowned continents, the retreating coastlines, the city’s elevation, the evacuation of surviving populations into the floating habitats. Then the image sharpened, and she saw lights.

They clustered along the former coast of West Africa. They threaded the eastern edge of South America. They formed bright chains around the Mediterranean basin and scattered points across the old British mainland. Some were large enough to be cities. Others appeared in careful grids, each cluster surrounded by dark fields.

Cultivated land.

Mara stepped closer.

The survey was dated eight years after the Continuance.

The official lessons said the continents had become uninhabitable before Lumen rose. The official maps showed no permanent settlements beyond the authorized extraction zones. Yet this image showed roads, farms, ports, and power stations. Not ruins. Not isolated emergency camps. Patterns of habitation.

A second layer opened automatically, displaying atmospheric measurements. The surface was not healthy. Toxic particulate concentrations were high in regions beneath Lumen’s climate network. Rainfall had become erratic. But the survey’s conclusion was unmistakable: human communities remained viable, and in several areas were rebuilding.

Mara’s hands went cold.

She searched for a falsification marker. The file carried a survey seal, three independent instrument signatures, and a chain of transmissions routed through observation satellites. One signature had been manually blacked out. Another had been replaced with the word DECOMMISSIONED.

Outdated, she thought.

The satellite might have malfunctioned. The lights could be industrial fires. The fields could be abandoned test plots. The report might be a draft, a hopeful error that wiser authorities had rejected.

She repeated each explanation until it sounded almost reasonable.

Then she saw the image of the British coast.

The old Thames basin was marked by a crescent of lights around a drowned transport hub. A note identified the location as TILBURY ELEVATION ZONE, with an estimated population of 18,400. Nearby fields were labeled reed filtration, salt-tolerant grain, and medicinal cultivation.

Eli’s treatment might exist there.

Mara touched the display. “No.”

The map did not change.

She copied the survey, the settlement index, and the medicinal cultivation note. The transfer completed at eighty-seven percent before the tablet gave a warning that made her blood stop.

SECONDARY AUTHENTICATION REQUIRED.

Someone else had connected to the archive.

From beyond the partition came the quiet scrape of a door opening.

Mara shut down the display. Darkness filled the room. She tucked the tablet beneath her shirt and crouched beside the circular table, listening.

Footsteps entered the archive aisle. Not the humming movement of a drone. Human steps, measured and unhurried.

A beam of light passed beneath the partition.

Mara reached for the maintenance hatch behind her. It was locked. She tried the copied credential. Nothing. She tried the emergency code. The screen remained dark.

The footsteps stopped outside.

A voice, young and male, spoke into the darkness.

“I know someone is in there.”

Mara pressed one hand over her mouth. She could hear the person breathing through the thin partition.

The voice continued, quieter now. “If you’re security, you would have announced yourself.”

The door began to open.

Mara’s fingers closed around the loose data wafer she had taken from the floor. She had no weapon, no route out, and no explanation that would survive an interrogation. Behind the opening door, a figure’s shadow stretched across the archive floor.

She raised the wafer between two fingers, as if it could become a blade.

The door opened wider.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old apprentice cartographer from the Ring Twelve lower residential sector of Lumen, currently hiding inside the sealed archive beneath the Office of Cartography after entering illegally after hours. Her immediate goal is to find treatment or medical knowledge that could help stabilize Eli, while concealing her discoveries and escaping the archive. She lives with her mother Sela and younger brother Eli; Sela is considering selling household citizenship credits for Eli’s care, and Eli knows Mara has made another dangerous promise. Mara knows the archive contains suppressed pre-Continuance records, has copied respiratory exposure studies and incomplete dosage data comparable to Lumenex, and has discovered authenticated satellite surveys showing inhabited mainland settlements, cultivated land, and medicinal cultivation near Tilbury, contradicting Lumen’s official history. She also knows automated security has recorded her access and that an unidentified young man has entered the archive. She possesses her work tablet with private map layers and copied files, drafting folio, apprentice wrist tag, borrowed maintenance coveralls, copied emergency maintenance credential, and a loose data wafer. She is frightened, exhilarated, suspicious, and struggling to explain away evidence that could overturn her understanding of the world.

set.name: Sela Venn
set.description: Mara and Eli’s mother, living in the Ring Twelve family apartment and working exhausting filtration-membrane shifts. She is asleep at home after leaving the citizenship ledger and black transfer key near her, while considering whether to sell household credits to obtain Eli’s treatment. She loves and protects Mara and Eli but is frightened that Mara’s unauthorized actions could threaten housing, power allocation, certification, and legal protections. She possesses repair tools, filtration materials, utility worker wrist tag, family citizenship ledger, renewal papers, and black transfer key; she is exhausted, anxious, and unaware that Mara has entered the sealed archive.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Twelve-year-old Mara’s younger brother, living in the Ring Twelve family apartment with Sela and suffering a sharply worsening chronic respiratory condition. He remains dependent on a breathing tube and portable concentrator, weak and unstable while awaiting official review. He woke before Mara left and recognized that she was secretly going somewhere dangerous, warning her not to get caught. He knows the clinic denied him effective treatment and that Sela is considering a citizenship-credit transfer. He possesses his breathing equipment and remains witty, perceptive, frightened, and in urgent need of treatment.

set.name: Tomas Rusk
set.description: Not yet identified by name in the narrative; a young male intruder who has just entered the sealed archive beneath the Office of Cartography while Mara is inside. His location is the archive entrance or adjoining aisle, and his immediate goal, knowledge, relationships, possessions, and physical condition remain unknown. He has announced that he knows someone is present and appears to distinguish himself from ordinary security, making him a potentially dangerous but deliberate human investigator.

set.name: Nia Vale

Mara used a copied emergency maintenance credential to enter the sealed archive beneath the Office of Cartography after hours and evade its automated security system.
Mara found and copied pre-Continuance medical exposure studies, incomplete treatment dosage data, and access logs related to respiratory compounds comparable to Lumenex.

Mara discovered authenticated satellite surveys showing surviving mainland settlements, cultivated land, and medicinal cultivation near the former Tilbury transport hub, contradicting Lumen’s official history that the continents were uninhabitable.
A second, unidentified person entered the sealed archive while Mara was copying the environmental surveys and confronted her from beyond a partition.
Mara and the person who entered the archive will confront one another over the copied files and the concealed mainland settlements, beginning a dangerous reluctant alliance.

chapters.name: The Boy from Broadcast
chapters.content:
The door opened wider.

The stranger stood in the gap with one hand on the manual wheel and the other raised to shield his eyes from the emergency light. He was about Mara’s age, perhaps a year older, though the smooth cut of his charcoal jacket made him seem more distant than old. A silver communications badge rested at his throat. His hair, dark and carefully trimmed, had come loose above one eyebrow. He looked like someone who belonged in a bright room where people were expected to listen.

Mara kept the data wafer between her fingers.

“Put that down,” he said.

“You first.”

His gaze moved over her borrowed coveralls, the tablet hidden beneath them, and finally the wafer. “That isn’t a weapon.”

“Then you have nothing to worry about.”

“I’m not the one hiding in a sealed archive.”

“You’re in it too.”

“I have authorization.”

“From whom?”

The boy hesitated. It was brief, but Mara saw it. His confidence had a seam in it.

“From the Broadcast Ministry,” he said.

“That isn’t authorization.”

“It is when the archive contains records classified by the Council.”

Mara felt the copied files beneath her shirt as if they had become hot metal. “Classified as what?”

“Restricted.”

“That’s not a classification.”

“It is the only one you need to know.”

He stepped inside. The door sighed shut behind him, cutting off the aisle and the faint mechanical hum of the searching drone. He did not look surprised to find her. That frightened Mara more than the drone had.

“You’re an apprentice,” he said.

“Maintenance worker.”

“Your boots have cartography dust on them.”

She glanced down. Fine white grit from the office stairwell clung to the seams. He noticed everything without appearing to look. A communications aide, she thought. Someone trained to watch faces while pretending to watch signals.

“Who are you?” she asked.

“Someone who can report you.”

“Then report me.”

His expression tightened. “You think I won’t?”

“No. I think you came down here alone because you don’t want anyone to know what you found.”

The silence between them changed shape.

Beyond the partition, the security drone chimed. Its beam moved along the shelves, searching for the sound of the wafer. The stranger turned his head toward it.

“What did you copy?” he asked.

“Nothing that belongs to you.”

“Everything in this archive belongs to the city.”

“The city doesn’t know it exists.”

“Because the city doesn’t need to know everything.”

Mara laughed once, without humor. “That’s convenient.”

“It’s necessary.”

“Necessary for whom?”

“For everyone who would die if frightened people started making decisions about systems they don’t understand.”

“You mean decisions like whether a child gets medicine?”

His eyes returned to her face. “What child?”

“Mine.”

The word escaped before she could stop it. She hated that he could now place the urgency in her voice, could fit her into a familiar category: desperate dependent, lower-ring family, predictable risk.

The drone struck the outer partition with a hard metallic tap. The lights in the archive went dark, then red. A system voice announced, “Unauthorized persons remain in secured storage. Response team dispatched.”

The boy’s composure broke.

“Response team?” Mara whispered.

“Did you trigger the review?”

“It recorded me before you arrived.”

“Then why is it searching this sector?”

“Because you connected to the terminal.”

He swore under his breath and moved toward the circular table. “How long?”

“Until what?”

“Until they lock the archive down.”

“You tell me. You have authorization.”

“I have a temporary inquiry code.”

“Which is not authorization.”

“Stop repeating that.”

“Stop pretending you’re in control.”

He pulled a slim black device from his jacket and pressed it against the wall display. The screen flickered alive. For an instant, the satellite image of the mainland appeared between bands of static: lights along the coast, dark fields, the marked crescent of Tilbury.

The boy stared at it.

“You saw this,” he said.

“I saw what was there.”

“No. You saw a file.”

“A file showing settlements.”

“An unverified survey.”

“With three instrument signatures.”

“Instrument signatures can be forged.”

“Then why are you here?”

His jaw worked. He looked again at the lights. “The Broadcast Ministry flagged the file as a containment concern.”

“Containment.”

“It means the information could destabilize public confidence.”

“It means you know it’s true.”

“It means I know the Council thinks people should not be allowed to act on it.”

Mara stepped closer. “That isn’t the same thing.”

“It is the same thing when the consequences are real.”

“Maps aren’t supposed to make people confident.”

“What are they supposed to do?”

“Show where things are.”

“Maps show what their makers decide is relevant.”

“Then your maps are lies.”

He flinched as though she had struck him.

The admission surprised her. The boy looked toward the survey again, and when he spoke his voice had lost its practiced certainty.

“My mother was sick,” he said.

Mara said nothing.

“She had a respiratory illness. Not the kind they tell people is unavoidable. There was a treatment. A compound from an older medical program. The hospital said it was experimental, then said it was unavailable, then said her condition was too advanced.”

The red light pulsed over his face.

“How long ago?” Mara asked.

“Three years.”

“And your family couldn’t get it?”

“My family could get anything.” His mouth twisted. “That was what I believed. My father had ministers at our table. Council physicians came to the apartment. They brought equipment and spoke in careful voices. But the treatment was never approved for her case. By the time approval came, she couldn’t breathe without support.”

The drone tapped the partition again.

“Did she die?”

“Yes.”

He said it plainly, but his hand had closed around the black device so tightly that his knuckles showed white.

“Then why defend them?” Mara asked.

“Because I don’t know whether the treatment would have worked.”

“You said there was one.”

“I said there was a treatment. I don’t know if it was safe. I don’t know whether the records were complete. I don’t know whether the people who withheld it were cruel, frightened, or simply right about the risks.”

“You don’t know because they kept the records from you.”

His eyes lifted to hers.

“And you think showing everyone every fragment will save them?”

“I think people have the right to see what decides whether they live.”

“That isn’t a right the city can afford.”

“Then what does it afford?”

He looked at the tablet under her shirt. “You came for medical records.”

“For my brother.”

“What’s wrong with him?”

“Chronic exposure damage. The clinic calls it noncompliant pulmonary decline.”

“That’s a classification, not a diagnosis.”

“Exactly.”

A deep vibration passed through the floor. Somewhere above them, a security gate slammed shut. Mara pictured the response team descending the stairwell, sealed doors closing one after another. If they found her with the copied files, her certification would disappear. Sela could lose the apartment. Eli might be transferred somewhere no one could reach him.

The boy moved to the wall beside the partition and opened a narrow service panel. “There’s a maintenance crawlspace.”

“You said you had authorization.”

“I also know the building.”

“Why help me?”

“I’m not helping you. I’m avoiding an arrest in a room full of records my father ordered sealed.”

“Your father?”

He looked at her, measuring whether the name would mean anything. “Minister Rusk.”

Mara knew the voice before she remembered the face: the smooth nightly broadcasts, the assurances that Lumen remained humanity’s final refuge, the warnings about surface raiders and contaminated shores. Minister Rusk had been speaking to the city for most of her childhood.

“You’re his son.”

“Tomas Rusk.”

“The broadcast boy.”

His expression hardened. “I’m a junior communications aide.”

“You’re the boy who appears behind him when he announces new restrictions.”

“I appear behind a great many people.”

“Not people who get medicine.”

“Not this again.”

“It never stopped being this.”

For a second they faced one another in the red-lit archive, each holding a different version of the city. Mara saw the ration queues, the clinic cabinet, Eli’s ribs lifting beneath his blanket. Tomas seemed to see riots, broken pumps, crowds pressing against doors that could not be reopened once breached.

Then footsteps sounded beyond the partition.

Tomas seized Mara’s wrist and pulled her toward the service panel.

She jerked free. “Touch me again and I’ll—”

“Be quiet.”

A voice outside called, “Archive personnel, identify yourselves.”

Tomas opened the panel. Behind it, a narrow shaft descended between the archive wall and the office’s old ventilation trunk. The metal smelled of oil and cold dust.

“Get in.”

“After you.”

He slid into the shaft, then turned sideways to make room. Mara followed, pulling the panel nearly closed behind her. They crouched shoulder to shoulder in darkness while the response team entered the room.

Through the gap, she saw two gray security uniforms and the hovering drone. One officer carried a scanner. The other held a shock baton.

“Thermal traces indicate two subjects,” the scanner officer said.

Tomas leaned close to Mara’s ear. “There was one subject.”

“Your device—”

“Can scramble a thermal reading for twelve seconds.”

“Why didn’t you do that before?”

“Because I didn’t know you were here.”

The drone floated toward the panel. Tomas pressed his black device against the shaft wall. A pulse shivered through the metal. The drone’s light went white, then spun in a confused circle.

“Signal interference,” the officer said. “Search the adjacent stacks.”

The team moved away.

Mara could hear Tomas breathing. He smelled faintly of rain and the sharp mineral scent of broadcast equipment. “You’re not security,” she whispered.

“I told you.”

“You’re not a loyal investigator either.”

“Keep your voice down.”

“You came for the survey.”

“I came for a file connected to an emergency transmission.”

“What transmission?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“Then you don’t know what you’re defending.”

“I know enough to know that you’re carrying stolen data.”

“And you want it.”

“I want to see what you copied.”

“Why?”

“Because you said there were medical records.”

“I said there might be something for my brother.”

“And the mainland survey?”

Mara thought of the lights beneath the clouds. “That too.”

He was silent.

The officers returned. One tested the service panel. Mara felt Tomas tense beside her. The latch shifted a fraction.

He lifted two fingers, then pointed down the shaft. Mara followed his gesture. A second opening showed a dim line of blue light several meters below.

They would have to crawl.

The panel began to open.

Mara moved first. She pressed herself into the shaft and crawled over the ridged metal, keeping the tablet tight against her chest. Tomas followed, one hand braced against the wall and the other holding the scrambling device. Behind them, the panel clanged fully open.

“Nothing here,” an officer said.

“Check the lower trunk.”

Mara reached the blue-lit opening and dropped through. She landed in an unused conduit room beneath the archive. Tomas came after her, less gracefully, striking his shoulder against the frame.

The room held a row of maintenance terminals, most dead. One still displayed a route diagram. Mara recognized the branching lines immediately.

“T-17,” she said.

Tomas glanced at it. “You know this route?”

“I copied its coordinates months ago.”

“Where does it lead?”

“External observation infrastructure. Maybe.”

“Maybe isn’t useful.”

“It’s more useful than the official map.”

He almost smiled, but the sound of boots overhead erased it.

Mara crossed to the terminal and entered the route code. The diagram unfolded through layers of abandoned corridors, ending at a service lift marked OUTER WEATHER ARRAY. A second branch ran toward an old communications relay.

Tomas studied the display. “This connects to a ministry signal trunk.”

“And?”

“And I can get you out through the office’s maintenance exit.”

“What do you want?”

“The files.”

“No.”

“The medical records, at least.”

“You’ll report me.”

“I could have done that already.”

“You threatened to.”

“I was trying to make you give me the tablet.”

“Very reassuring.”

He faced her fully. “I won’t report you if you let me examine what you copied. I want the survey and the medical data. I want to know whether either is real.”

“You’ll keep copies.”

“Yes.”

“For your father?”

“For me.”

“And if you decide it’s dangerous?”

“Then I’ll tell you before I do anything.”

“That’s not a promise.”

“No,” Tomas said. “It’s the most honest offer I have.”

Above them, the security team began forcing the lower hatch. Metal groaned. Mara imagined Eli waiting beneath the concentrator’s clicking rhythm, Sela’s hand curled around the transfer key. She had entered the archive seeking one kind of proof and found another: proof that the world was larger than Lumen’s walls, proof that even the powerful could lose someone while medicine sat behind locked doors.

She removed the tablet from beneath her coveralls but did not hand it over.

“You get the records,” she said. “You do not transmit them, alter them, or show them to anyone without telling me first.”

“That’s an impossible condition.”

“Then leave me here.”

Tomas considered her. “You really believe a map should show everything.”

“I believe people should know what they’re standing on.”

His gaze dropped to the tablet. “And I believe some truths need a route before they need an audience.”

“Then find the route.”

The hatch above them buckled inward.

Tomas reached for the terminal and entered a sequence of ministry codes. The dead conduit room came alive. A maintenance door opened at the far end, revealing a narrow stair that rose toward the dark office.

“Move,” he said.

Mara followed him up.

They emerged behind a bank of dormant drafting stations as alarms began to pulse through the building. Tomas led her across the office without hesitation, through a records room and into a service corridor she had never seen on the apprentice plans. At its end, a freight lift waited with its doors open.

“Where does this go?”

“Lower maintenance ring.”

“Not the outer weather array?”

“Not tonight.”

The lift shuddered downward. For several floors they stood without speaking. The city’s buoyancy engines beat beneath them, steady and immense.

At Ring Twelve, Tomas stopped the lift before the public platform. He handed Mara a small black contact wafer.

“Tomorrow,” he said. “Same hour. Bring the files.”

“You’ll bring what?”

“I’ll investigate the medical references through the ministry index.”

“Why should I trust you?”

“You shouldn’t.”

The doors opened onto a dim service passage.

Tomas stepped out, then looked back. “But if the records are real, your brother may not have much time.”

Mara’s fingers closed around the wafer.

“Neither does the city,” she said.

For the first time, Tomas had no answer.

He turned and disappeared into the maintenance shadows. Mara waited until the lift doors shut, then began the walk home with the copied world hidden against her ribs.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old apprentice cartographer from the Ring Twelve lower residential sector of Lumen, now back in or near the Ring Twelve service passages after escaping the sealed archive. Her immediate goals are to protect Eli, meet Tomas again, determine whether the copied respiratory records can help Eli, and understand the mainland settlements shown in the survey. She believes maps should show reality and that people deserve access to knowledge affecting their survival, but she recognizes that releasing evidence without a route or plan could create danger. She has copied pre-Continuance respiratory studies, incomplete dosage data comparable to Lumenex, authenticated satellite surveys showing inhabited mainland settlements and medicinal cultivation near Tilbury, access logs, the T-17 route diagram, and related files on her work tablet. She also possesses a drafting folio, borrowed maintenance coveralls, utility worker wrist tag, copied emergency maintenance credential, loose data wafer, and Tomas’s black contact wafer. She knows Tomas Rusk’s identity, his position as a junior communications aide, his relationship to Minister Rusk, his mother’s death from a potentially treatable respiratory illness, and his conditional offer to investigate ministry medical records. She is frightened, suspicious, angry at Lumen’s secrecy, and cautiously committed to the alliance.

set.name: Sela Venn
set.description: Mara and Eli’s mother, living in the Ring Twelve family apartment and working exhausting filtration-membrane shifts. She remains asleep or resting at home with the citizenship ledger and black transfer key nearby, considering whether to sell household credits for Eli’s treatment. She loves and protects Mara and Eli but is frightened that Mara’s unauthorized actions could threaten housing, power allocation, certification, and legal protections. She does not yet know Mara entered the sealed archive or allied with Tomas. She possesses repair tools, filtration materials, utility worker wrist tag, family citizenship ledger, renewal papers, and black transfer key; she is exhausted, anxious, and vulnerable to further official pressure.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Twelve-year-old Mara’s younger brother, living in the Ring Twelve family apartment with Sela and suffering a sharply worsening chronic respiratory condition. He remains dependent on a breathing tube and portable concentrator, weak and unstable while awaiting official review. He knows Mara left on a dangerous mission but does not know she found possible treatment records or evidence of living mainland communities. He possesses his breathing equipment and remains witty, perceptive, frightened, and in urgent need of treatment.

set.name: Tomas Rusk
set.description: Young junior communications aide and son of Council Minister Rusk, currently separated from Mara in the Ring Twelve maintenance passages after helping her escape the sealed archive response team. He entered the archive under a temporary Ministry inquiry code to investigate classified files and recognizes that the survey and medical records have been deliberately contained. His father’s status gives him access to Ministry indexes and signal systems, but he distrusts the Council more than he admits: his mother died three years earlier from a respiratory illness after his elite family failed to secure a potentially effective treatment. He believes dangerous truths may need a controlled route before public release, while Mara believes maps and survival information should be visible. He possesses a black communications device, ministry codes, and a contact wafer given to Mara. He is shaken, defensive, curious, and bound to a conditional alliance: he will investigate the restricted medical references and not immediately report Mara, while she will let him examine copies of the survey and medical files.

The archive intruder identified himself as Tomas Rusk, a junior communications aide and son of Minister Rusk, and revealed that his mother died after a respiratory illness despite his family’s elite access and a potentially relevant treatment.

Tomas helped Mara evade the archive response team through a concealed maintenance route, and they formed a conditional alliance: Mara would share her copied survey and medical files while Tomas investigated the ministry records and withheld immediate reporting.
Mara and Tomas discovered that the hidden T-17 route connects abandoned archive infrastructure to an outer weather array and a Ministry communications relay.
Mara and Tomas will meet again to compare the copied mainland survey and medical records, with Tomas investigating the ministry index for treatment evidence.
Tomas will use his Broadcast Ministry access to investigate the restricted medical references and determine whether a treatment comparable to Lumenex exists.

chapters.name: The World Below
chapters.content:
Mara did not sleep.

She lay beside the wall in the family apartment, listening to Eli’s concentrator click and sigh. Each breath it gave him sounded borrowed. Sela had fallen asleep in her work clothes at the table, one hand resting on the citizenship ledger, the black transfer key beneath her palm. The apartment lights had dimmed to their night setting, turning the ceiling into a gray imitation of dawn.

Mara kept Tomas’s contact wafer under her pillow.

At the first cycle bell, she rose. Eli opened his eyes.

“Did you find anything?” he whispered.

“Not yet.”

“That means yes.”

“You’re supposed to be sleeping.”

“I’m supposed to be breathing. I can multitask.”

His smile became a cough. Mara crouched beside him until it passed. The tube at his nose trembled with every shallow inhale.

“I’ll find something,” she said.

Eli studied her face. “Something for me, or something that makes you angry?”

She had no answer that would not frighten him. She adjusted the blanket and left before Sela woke.

In the washroom, she splashed cold water over her face and looked at herself in the cracked mirror. Archive dust still marked the seam of her borrowed coveralls. Beneath her shirt, the data wafer pressed against her ribs. It contained a coast she had been taught was dead, but the lie felt less solid than the people sleeping around it. She wondered how many maps she had drawn that were not wrong by accident, but by instruction.

The maintenance passage beneath Ring Twelve smelled of wet metal and overheated wiring. Mara reached the disused pump chamber at the appointed hour. Tomas was already there, seated on an overturned conduit case, his black communications device open across his knees.

“You’re late,” he said.

“The city clock says otherwise.”

“The city clock is controlled by the Ministry.”

“Then it has learned from you.”

He glanced up, and for an instant she saw the almost-smile from the archive. It vanished quickly.

“I searched the medical index,” he said. “The compound you copied is listed under several names. One is Lumenex.”

Mara’s pulse struck hard. “How many doses?”

“That depends on what you mean by listed.”

“Tomas.”

“The original program was not abandoned because it failed. It was transferred.”

“To where?”

“Atmospheric adaptation.”

The words seemed to make the chamber colder.

He turned the device so she could see. A chain of ministry references filled the screen, most blacked out, others marked with red containment seals. Beside one entry was a note: RESPIRATORY COMPOUND—RESTRICTED TO CONTINUANCE EXPOSURE STUDIES.

“Continuance,” Mara said. “The city’s founding project?”

“The program that established Lumen’s stabilizers and the upper atmospheric shield.”

“Why would a respiratory medicine be part of that?”

“Because the shield changed the air.”

He tapped another file. It opened reluctantly, revealing a technical table. Concentrations, wind vectors, particulate dispersal. Mara recognized the symbols from the environmental surveys: not simply weather measurements, but emissions patterns.

“Show me the map,” she said.

Tomas hesitated, then overlaid the table on the copied satellite image. The picture of the British coast expanded. Blue-gray water filled the old Thames basin, but along the edges were widening bands of green and brown. At first Mara thought they were errors. Then the labels resolved: reed cultivation, salt-resistant grain, freshwater collection, habitation clusters.

The coastline had moved.

“Those are from different years,” Tomas said. “The survey drones flew the same routes every six months. The oceans around the old coast are receding.”

Mara leaned closer. “The official lessons say the flood line is still rising.”

“The lessons use projections from before the stabilizer network reached full capacity.”

“Why?”

“Because the updated projections are sealed.”

He opened the drone reports one at a time. A settlement built around the elevated remains of Tilbury. Farms arranged in long dark strips above the old rail embankment. Fog nets stretched between towers. A clinic powered by tidal turbines. The images were grainy, but people moved through them: a child carrying a yellow bucket, two figures repairing a roof, a line of boats entering a channel between reeds.

Mara stared until the pixels blurred.

“They’re alive,” she said.

“Yes.”

“They have farms.”

“Yes.”

“They have medicine.”

Tomas looked at the respiratory file. “Some of them do.”

A report opened beneath his hand. It described a plant-derived treatment for particulate injury, developed by a coastal medical cooperative and tested on children living near the southern arrays. The formula was incomplete in the archive copy, but the treatment family matched the references connected to Lumenex.

Mara seized the device. “This could stabilize Eli.”

“It could.”

“You said there was a treatment.”

“I said the records point to one. We don’t know the dosage, the contraindications, or whether the clinic has the equipment to administer it.”

“Then we get the rest.”

“From the mainland?”

“From wherever it is.”

Tomas took the device back. “You’re thinking about leaving.”

“I’m thinking about my brother.”

“They would stop us before we reached an external deck.”

“Then find another route.”

“That’s what the T-17 corridor is for.”

He loaded Mara’s restored route diagram. The line from the archive ran beyond Lumen’s outer frame to a weather array suspended over the dark Atlantic. From there, a second path descended through a relay station toward Tilbury.

“It was designed for survey crews,” Tomas said. “The descent infrastructure was decommissioned after the mainland became officially uninhabitable.”

“Officially.”

“Don’t make that word do all the work.”

“Then tell me what happened.”

Tomas looked away. He had seemed composed in the archive, but now his fingers kept moving over the edge of the device.

“The first atmospheric stabilizers were meant to regulate storms and keep Lumen aloft. They worked by redirecting heat and pressure. The Council expanded the system when the mainland refused evacuation.”

“Refused?”

“Some communities did. Others were never offered a choice.”

He opened a maintenance memorandum. Its author had marked several paragraphs for deletion. Mara read the surviving lines: concentrated carbon discharge, lower-atmosphere particulate burden, projected mortality in coastal exposure zones.

Below them was a sentence stamped ACCEPTABLE CONTAINMENT COST.

Mara read it twice.

“What does that mean?”

Tomas’s voice was flat. “It means they knew.”

The pump chamber seemed to tilt. The city’s engines beat through the walls, massive and regular, like a heart that had never asked what blood it consumed.

“All this time,” Mara said. “The storms. The poisoned air. The illnesses.”

“Some of it was unavoidable.”

“Some.”

“The system prevented Lumen from falling.”

“And pushed the damage down.”

He did not deny it.

Mara looked again at the photographs. The cultivated strips along the coast. The clinic roof. The yellow bucket in a child’s hand. She thought of Eli’s ribs, of Halden’s cabinet of Lumenex doses, of Sela counting citizenship credits beneath a flickering apartment light.

“What is the Crown Seal?” she asked.

Tomas’s face changed.

“Where did you see that?”

“In the maintenance index.”

“That file is beyond my access.”

“You have Ministry codes.”

“I have junior Ministry codes.”

“Then use them.”

He sat still for a long moment. Finally he entered a sequence, paused at a warning, and entered another. The device displayed a black field. A title appeared in white.

CROWN SEAL: PERMANENT ATMOSPHERIC ENCLOSURE AND RESOURCE CONTAINMENT.

Mara felt the blood leave her hands.

The document was a Council memorandum dated nine years earlier. It described a sealed perimeter around Lumen, an intensified stabilizer network, and a permanent restriction on all external transit. The city would become independent of mainland conditions, the memorandum said. Its food, air, and energy systems would be secured within a controlled envelope.

The diagrams showed the enclosure as a shining ring around Lumen.

The projections showed everything beyond it darkening.

“Tomas,” Mara said. “What does permanent mean?”

“No descent. No outside exchange. No interference from surface communities.”

“And the emissions?”

He scrolled. The language grew more technical and more horrifying. Increased thermal discharge. Concentrated particulate release. Accelerated oceanic and atmospheric disruption beyond the containment perimeter. The Crown Seal would protect the city by making recovery outside it nearly impossible.

A final authorization block bore the Council’s seal.

GLOBAL ECOLOGICAL COLLAPSE IS AN ACCEPTABLE COST FOR HUMAN CONTINUANCE WITHIN THE LUMEN ENVELOPE.

Mara pushed away from the screen.

“They’re going to do it.”

“The activation date is redacted.”

“They’re going to do it.”

Tomas closed the file. “If the memorandum is still active.”

“You don’t believe that.”

“I believe the Council has abandoned enough plans to make a pattern. I don’t know which ones survived.”

“Then find out.”

His expression sharpened. “You want to expose this.”

“I want to get the medicine.”

He stared at her.

Mara heard her own words and hated how small they sounded beside the ruined world on the screen. But Eli was twelve. Eli was at home, breathing borrowed air. The settlements, the emissions, the Crown Seal—all of it was real, and none of it changed the fact that her brother might die before the city’s history could be corrected.

“We can copy the files,” Tomas said. “Send them through channels the Ministry can’t contain.”

“Can we get Eli treated that way?”

“No.”

“Then I don’t care who sees the truth yet.”

“That’s not what you said yesterday.”

“Yesterday I thought truth might be enough.”

She folded her arms around herself. “It isn’t. A map can show a road, but it can’t carry someone down it.”

Tomas looked toward the sealed door. “If we go to the mainland, we may not come back.”

“If we stay, the clinic will keep Eli sick because our family has the wrong number beside its name.”

“They could arrest you.”

“They could arrest us for breathing incorrectly.”

He gave a short, pained laugh. Then he brought the medical file back onto the screen.

“There’s one more reference,” he said. “A relay hospital near Tilbury. The treatment was developed there before the Council cut external communications.”

“Near the settlement in the survey?”

“Possibly.”

“Can you contact them?”

“Not directly. The old weather array has a ministry relay. If T-17 still functions, I can route a query through it.”

“And if it doesn’t?”

“Then we find another way.”

It was the first time he had said it without sounding as though he were trying to persuade himself.

Mara copied the medical references, the drone reports, the emissions tables, and the Crown Seal memorandum onto a new wafer. Her hands shook only once, when the authorization block transferred. She made three copies and gave one to Tomas.

“Keep it hidden,” she said.

“I know.”

“No, you know how to keep a secret for the Ministry. This is different.”

His eyes met hers. “I know the difference now.”

A warning tone sounded from his device. Someone had queried his access code.

“They’ve noticed,” he said.

“Who?”

“Ministry security. Maybe my father’s office.”

Mara thought of Sela asleep beside the citizenship ledger. “I have to go home.”

“If your access is flagged, they may already be watching your apartment.”

“Then I need to know before they reach it.”

Tomas stood and shut down the terminal. “Meet me at the T-17 junction after the next dark cycle.”

“You’re coming?”

“I’m the only one who can open the Ministry relay.”

“That wasn’t an answer.”

He hesitated. “Yes.”

They climbed through the service passage together. At the junction, where the route divided toward Ring Twelve and the abandoned lift, Mara stopped.

“Don’t send the files,” she said.

“Not yet.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

“The world below can wait one day.”

Tomas looked at the dark line of the T-17 corridor. “Maybe it can’t.”

Mara thought of the memorandum’s sentence, cold and official, reducing coastlines and children to a cost that someone else had accepted.

“Eli can’t wait,” she said.

She went toward home, carrying the treatment references beneath her shirt and the weight of the living world in her mind. Behind her, Tomas remained at the junction, staring into the corridor that led downward and outward, toward a truth neither of them was ready to release—and toward a city that had already begun deciding who would be sacrificed to keep it in the sky.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old apprentice cartographer from Ring Twelve, currently leaving the disused pump chamber and returning toward the family apartment after meeting Tomas at the T-17 junction. Her immediate goal is to obtain treatment for Eli, using the newly discovered medical references and possibly the Tilbury relay, while postponing public release of the evidence. She is allied with Tomas but does not fully trust him. She now knows the copied surveys are authentic enough to show receding coastal waters, inhabited mainland settlements, farms, clinics, and medicinal research; she knows Lumen’s stabilizers redirect greenhouse gases and toxic particulates toward the mainland; she has read the Council memorandum describing that suffering as an acceptable containment cost; and she knows of the Crown Seal plan to permanently enclose Lumen and accelerate ecological collapse. She possesses her work tablet, copied medical and environmental files, multiple new data-wafer copies including the Crown Seal memorandum, drafting folio, maintenance coveralls, utility wrist tag, emergency credential, and Tomas’s contact wafer. She remains frightened, furious, morally shaken, and focused on Eli rather than public revelation.

set.description: Mara and Eli’s mother, currently asleep or resting in the Ring Twelve family apartment after a filtration-membrane shift, with the citizenship ledger and black transfer key nearby. She does not yet know Mara has decoded the archive files, learned the mainland is inhabited, or formed a plan with Tomas. Her immediate goal remains securing Eli’s treatment without losing the household’s housing, power allocation, certification, or legal protections. set.description: Twelve-year-old Mara’s younger brother, currently in the Ring Twelve family apartment with Sela, dependent on a breathing tube and portable concentrator while his chronic respiratory condition worsens. He knows Mara is pursuing something dangerous but does not know she found a possible mainland treatment or proof that the mainland is inhabited. His immediate need is urgent stabilization. set.name: Tomas Rusk
set.description: Young junior communications aide and son of Minister Rusk, currently at or near the T-17 junction in the Ring Twelve maintenance passages after meeting Mara. His immediate goals are to route a query through the old Ministry relay toward the Tilbury hospital, help obtain treatment for Eli, determine whether the Crown Seal remains active, and keep the copied evidence hidden temporarily. He remains conditionally allied with Mara; their trust has strengthened but both expect betrayal to remain possible. He knows the mainland surveys document living settlements and receding coastal waters, the stabilizer network’s harmful emissions, the Council’s acceptance of mainland suffering, the Crown Seal enclosure plan, and the existence of a potentially useful mainland respiratory treatment near Tilbury. He possesses his black communications device, Ministry access codes, one copy of the decoded files, and technical knowledge of the T-17 route and relay. He is shaken, defensive, increasingly distrustful of the Council, and committed to helping Mara despite the risk of Ministry detection.

Mara and Tomas decoded the copied files and confirmed that survey drones documented receding water around the former British coast, cultivated mainland farms, functioning clinics, and inhabited settlements near Tilbury.

The files revealed that Lumen’s atmospheric stabilizers redirect concentrated greenhouse gases and toxic particulates toward the mainland, with a Council memorandum explicitly calling the resulting suffering an acceptable containment cost.

Mara and Tomas discovered the Crown Seal plan for permanent atmospheric enclosure of Lumen, intensified emissions, and global ecological collapse outside the city, though its activation date remains unknown.
Tomas found restricted records indicating a mainland-developed respiratory treatment near Tilbury that may stabilize Eli, but the dosage and administration details remain incomplete.
Mara and Tomas will use the evidence of withheld treatment and falsified environmental records to seek Eli’s medicine before deciding whether to expose the Crown Seal publicly.
Mara and Tomas will attempt to reach or query the old Ministry relay along the T-17 corridor for treatment information connected to the Tilbury hospital.

chapters.name: A Bargain with the Clinic
chapters.content:
Mara reached the clinic before the first public bell, when the corridors smelled of disinfectant and boiled grain and the night attendants were still rubbing sleep from their eyes.

She had expected Tomas to be waiting at the service entrance. Instead, his message blinked on her contact wafer.

DELayed. MINISTRY QUERY. USE WEST ACCESS.

She read it twice. The words had been stripped of his usual caution. Mara slipped the wafer beneath her sleeve and entered through the public doors.

Administrator Halden was already there.

He stood behind the clinic counter in a gray coat, his hands folded over the cabinet that held the Lumenex. The cabinet’s glass reflected Mara’s face in fragments. Inside, the doses rested in their foam compartments, pale and orderly, each one labeled for a person who had not yet arrived.

“Apprentice Venn,” Halden said. “You have been advised not to return without an appointment.”

“My brother needs treatment.”

“Your brother was assessed.”

“He was denied.”

“He was assigned supportive care.”

“His lungs are failing.”

Halden’s expression did not change. “A difficult condition does not cancel civic procedure.”

Mara looked past him. Two attendants were arranging sealed trays. One glanced at her and quickly looked away.

“I know what is in that cabinet,” Mara said.

“Lumenex. Restricted stock.”

“I know what it is restricted for.”

“Then you understand why this conversation is over.”

“No.” Mara stepped closer to the counter. “I understand that your reports say the lower rings have no eligible cases, while the cabinet contains doses for patients who have not been examined. I understand that the public health summaries omit particulate exposure from the eastern arrays. I understand that you are marking children like my brother as low-value dependents while reserving treatment for citizens whose work credits are worth more.”

The room had gone quiet.

Halden’s fingers tightened against the counter. “Those are serious accusations.”

“They are documented.”

“By whom?”

Mara placed a data wafer on the counter. Not the original. One of Tomas’s copies, sealed in a plain maintenance sleeve.

“By your own records.”

Halden did not touch it. His eyes moved from the wafer to Mara and then toward the security lens above the entrance.

“You stole classified medical information.”

“I copied records that concern my brother’s life.”

“You entered an unauthorized archive.”

“You have no idea where I got this.”

“I have a very good idea.”

The lie between them was thin as membrane. Mara could hear the concentrator in her memory: click, sigh, click. Eli waiting at home. Sela waiting for her to return with either medicine or another explanation that would sound like surrender.

“Give him one dose,” Mara said. “You can record it as an emergency variance. You can say his symptoms worsened and I pressured you. You can blame me for everything except letting him die.”

Halden’s voice dropped. “You think this is a negotiation.”

“It is.”

“No. It is extortion.”

“Then call it that. Call the Council. When they arrive, I will tell them where the withheld doses are and why your health reports are false.”

For the first time, fear showed in his face—not fear for Eli, or for the people whose names filled the clinic’s unspoken waiting list, but fear of being seen by someone with power to examine his records.

“You will leave,” he said.

“Not without the treatment.”

“You are dismissed from the clinic grounds.”

“I’m not the patient.”

“Your family’s certification can be reviewed.”

“There it is.”

Halden reached beneath the counter. Mara expected an alarm. Instead he produced a thin black authorization strip and laid it beside the wafer.

“Your brother is not eligible for Lumenex under his current classification,” he said. “That can be changed. Your mother can transfer household credits. Or she can sign a dependent reassignment. The procedure is simple.”

Mara stared at the strip. “You’re offering to erase him from our household.”

“I’m describing available pathways.”

“You would call killing him a pathway.”

“I would call it preserving the family’s remaining benefits.”

She snatched the wafer from the counter. “You already have a record of this conversation.”

“Of course.”

“Then include the part where I asked for medicine and you offered to make my brother legally disappear.”

Halden tapped the security lens. “The Council will receive a complete report.”

“Good.”

She turned before her anger could make her careless. At the west access door, a red light changed to green. Tomas’s message had not been delayed. It had been a warning.

Mara ran.

The service corridor narrowed behind the clinic, its walls crowded with pipes and insulated conduits. She passed a maintenance crew without looking at them and reached the old junction where the public ventilation line crossed the medical transfer route. Tomas emerged from a hatch above her, landing badly and catching himself against the wall.

“Did you get the relay?” she asked.

“I got a response.”

“From Tilbury?”

“Not exactly.”

He held out his communications device. A string of routing codes scrolled across the screen. One line remained uncorrupted.

QUERY RECEIVED. TREATMENT POSSIBLE. PATIENT CONDITION AND DOSAGE REQUIRED. DO NOT USE COUNCIL CHANNELS.

Mara’s breath caught. “They answered.”

“Someone did. The relay is active.”

“Can they send the medicine?”

“Not through the city network. I asked for a dosage protocol. The connection dropped.”

“Then we need to ask again.”

“They already know we asked.”

A tone sounded behind them.

Not an alarm. A clinic priority signal.

Tomas’s face went still. “That’s a transfer order.”

“For Eli?”

He looked at the routing code. “Patient E-412. Ring Twelve family apartment. Respiratory trial candidate.”

Mara felt the corridor tilt beneath her feet. “They can’t move him.”

“They can if the Council has issued a medical seizure.”

“Then cancel it.”

“I don’t have that authority.”

“You’re a Ministry aide.”

“I read messages. I don’t command hospitals.”

“Your father does.”

The words struck him harder than she intended. Tomas closed the device and pushed past her toward the apartment route.

“I’ll stop it.”

They reached Ring Twelve as the public bell began. The family corridors were already filling with workers. A woman carrying a child moved aside for two white-suited hospital officers. Between them rolled a sealed transport cradle.

Sela stood in the apartment doorway.

Mara saw her mother’s face before she saw the cradle. Sela had one hand braced against the frame and the other pressed to Eli’s shoulder. His breathing tube ran beneath the collar of his sleep shirt. The portable concentrator rattled on the floor.

“No,” Mara said.

One of the officers lifted a tablet. “By order of the Central Medical Authority, patient E-412 is transferred to the North Research Ward for urgent atmospheric adaptation treatment.”

“He has not consented,” Sela said.

“Consent is waived under emergency classification.”

“He is twelve.”

“Which is why the ward has accepted him.”

Mara moved between the officers and the cradle. “He is not a trial subject.”

The officer’s eyes flicked to the data wafer under her sleeve. “Apprentice Venn, step aside.”

Behind Mara, Eli made a thin, frightened sound.

“Tell them to leave,” he whispered.

“I’m trying.”

The second officer reached for her arm. Sela struck his hand away with the black transfer key.

“Do not touch my daughter.”

The officer recoiled. A red mark appeared across his knuckles.

For one second, no one moved. Then the corridor filled with the hard click of arriving security boots.

Sela looked at Mara. It was not a mother’s look of permission. It was a mother’s look of calculation, as if she were already measuring how much of their life could be saved.

“Take the evidence,” Sela said.

Mara shook her head. “I’m not leaving you.”

“Take it.”

The security officers entered. Tomas stepped forward, displaying his Ministry device.

“I am Tomas Rusk, communications aide, provisional channel authority. This transfer is suspended pending—”

The lead officer scanned his face and lowered her weapon.

“Ministerial credentials revoked,” she said. “Stand away from the family.”

Tomas stared at the device. “That’s impossible.”

“Your access has been frozen.”

The hospital officers moved at once. Eli cried out as they lifted the cradle. Sela seized the side rail, and a guard twisted her arm behind her back.

“Stop!” Mara shouted.

The sound vanished beneath the corridor’s alarms. Doors sealed along the ring. The apartment lights flashed from white to emergency amber.

Sela was forced to her knees.

“Unauthorized interference with medical transfer,” the lead officer announced. “Attempted theft of restricted treatment. Detain the guardian.”

“Mum!”

Sela did not look at the officers. She looked only at Mara.

“Find him,” she said.

Eli’s cradle rolled away toward the lift. His fingers reached through the transparent panel, searching. Mara ran after him, but a barrier dropped from the ceiling between them. She struck it until her palms hurt.

The lift doors closed on Eli’s terrified face.

When Mara turned back, Sela was gone.

The corridor had emptied as quickly as it had filled. Neighbors watched from half-open doors, their expressions carefully blank. Tomas stood beneath the emergency light, his device dead in his hand.

“My father did this,” he said.

“Your father’s office did this.”

“It’s the same thing.”

“No.” Mara’s voice broke. “It isn’t the same thing to me.”

They ran to the family apartment.

The door was sealed with a Council band. A notice glowed across its surface:

HOUSEHOLD STATUS UNDER REVIEW.
PROPERTY ACCESS SUSPENDED.
CITIZENSHIP CREDITS: FROZEN.

Mara placed her wrist tag against the lock. Denied.

Sela’s repair tools were inside. Eli’s spare breathing cartridges. The ledger. The black transfer key, unless Sela had kept it in her hand when they took her.

Tomas read the notice. “They moved fast.”

“They knew before we came.”

“Halden reported us.”

“You said the Ministry query was delayed.”

“It was. My father’s office intercepted it.”

Mara rounded on him. “You told me you could protect the route.”

“I told you I could open it.”

“You told me your family had access.”

“They had access.” He struck the dead device against his palm. “Now they’re using it to close every door.”

The anger drained out of her, leaving something colder. “Can you get Sela?”

Tomas looked toward the lift where Eli had disappeared. “Not through my father.”

“Then through the hospital.”

“It’s a restricted ward.”

“You know the city’s routes.”

“I know the broadcasts.”

“You know enough.”

He closed his eyes. Behind them, the apartment seal hummed softly, preserving the family’s possessions for a family that no longer had legal access to them.

When he opened them, he had made a decision.

“There’s a maintenance authorization system beneath the hospital,” he said. “Old infrastructure. Before the Council divided clinical and service access, repairs were logged through a central queue. If I can generate an emergency order, the ward doors will recognize it for twelve minutes.”

“Twelve minutes to do what?”

“Reach the restricted levels. Find your mother. Find Eli.”

“And then?”

“Get out before the order is audited.”

“Where do we go?”

He looked at her. “Down.”

The word carried the weight of the T-17 corridor, the weather array, the relay hospital near Tilbury, and the living coast that waited beyond the city’s official edge.

Mara glanced once at the sealed apartment. Her home had become a locked room. Her brother had become a research subject. Her mother had become a detainee. The Council had answered her bargain with a larger one: obedience in exchange for the right to keep her family visible.

“Make the order,” she said.

Tomas pulled a maintenance slate from inside his coat. “I’ll need your route knowledge.”

“You’ll have it.”

“And after we free them, there may be no way back.”

Mara thought of the clinic cabinet, its doses waiting behind glass. She thought of Halden’s calm voice describing the removal of a dependent as a pathway. She thought of the message from Tilbury: treatment possible.

“Then we don’t come back.”

Tomas began to write.

He used the credentials of a nonexistent filtration failure, a pressure imbalance in the North Research Ward, and a repair crew that had been dissolved seven years earlier. Mara supplied the service routes, correcting the hospital’s official map where it concealed freight lifts and waste passages. Together they built a lie precise enough to pass through the city’s machinery.

At the final authorization field, Tomas hesitated.

“What?” Mara asked.

“This requires a sponsor.”

“Use your father.”

“He’ll see it.”

“Use his name anyway.”

Tomas looked toward the broadcast tower rising above the ring, its windows bright with morning announcements.

Then he entered: RUSK, MINISTERIAL OVERSIGHT.

The false order sealed itself with a green confirmation mark.

TEMPORARY ACCESS GRANTED.

Mara took the slate. Beneath the authorization was a route descending through the hospital’s service spine and ending at the old external transfer decks.

“The order gives access to the ward,” she said. “Not the decks.”

“I can extend it once we’re inside.”

“Can you?”

“No.”

It was the first honest answer he had given her that morning.

Mara folded the slate against her chest. “Then we improvise.”

Tomas retrieved a coil of cable and a pair of maintenance coats from a supply recess. Somewhere above them, the city’s announcement chimes began to play: Lumen secure, Lumen sufficient, Lumen eternal.

Mara pulled on the coat. The fabric smelled of oil and old rain.

“Ready?” Tomas asked.

“No.”

“Good.”

They entered the hospital through a waste conduit marked CLOSED FOR STRUCTURAL REVIEW. The false order opened the first door. Beyond it, the service spine descended into blue light and humming machinery. Mara carried the map. Tomas carried the forged authority. Between them lay the copied evidence, the names of the living below, and a plan that had become much larger than medicine without becoming less urgent.

At the bottom of the first stair, Mara heard a distant mechanical lock release.

Somewhere in the restricted levels, Eli was breathing borrowed air.

Somewhere else, Sela was waiting.

Mara started down.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old apprentice cartographer, currently disguised in a maintenance coat and descending through the North Research Hospital’s service spine with Tomas toward the restricted wards. Her immediate goals are to find and free Eli, locate and free Sela, obtain or preserve the mainland treatment information, and escape Lumen through external service infrastructure. She is allied with Tomas under extreme pressure but remains alert to his limitations and possible danger. She knows the copied medical and environmental files are authentic; the mainland is inhabited and has a potentially useful respiratory treatment; Lumen’s stabilizers harm the mainland; the Council accepts that harm; and the Crown Seal threatens global ecological collapse. She also knows Administrator Halden reported her clinic confrontation, Eli was seized for a respiratory trial, Sela was arrested, their apartment was sealed, and the family’s citizenship credits were frozen. She possesses her work tablet, copied files and data wafers, drafting folio, utility wrist tag, emergency credential, Tomas’s contact wafer, the forged maintenance slate, and a maintenance coat. She is furious, frightened, determined, and increasingly committed to leaving Lumen if necessary.

set.name: Sela Venn
set.description: Mara and Eli’s mother, currently detained somewhere in or near the North Research Hospital’s restricted levels after resisting Eli’s forced medical transfer. Her immediate need is protection from Council punishment and reunion with her children. She knows the clinic denied Eli treatment and that officials have now taken him under an emergency medical classification, but she does not know the full truth about the mainland or Crown Seal. She is separated from Mara and Eli, possesses or may still have the black transfer key after her arrest, and is exhausted, frightened, fiercely protective, and defiant.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Twelve-year-old Mara’s younger brother, currently confined in the North Research Ward as a respiratory trial candidate after being seized from the family apartment. He is dependent on breathing equipment and urgently needs stabilization; a mainland-developed treatment may help him, but dosage and administration remain incomplete. He knows Mara and Sela tried to protect him and that officials have taken him, but he does not know the full mainland truth. His breathing equipment may be attached to the transport cradle or ward apparatus. He is weak, frightened, perceptive, and trying to remain brave.

set.name: Tomas Rusk
set.description: Junior communications aide and son of Minister Rusk, currently disguised in a maintenance coat and descending through the North Research Hospital’s service spine with Mara. His immediate goals are to reach the restricted wards, rescue Sela and Eli, extend or evade the forged access authorization, and escape toward the T-17 route and external service decks. His conditional alliance with Mara has intensified, though she now knows his Ministry credentials were revoked and his family influence failed to protect them. He knows the mainland surveys and treatment references, the emissions memorandum, Crown Seal plan, active Tilbury relay, and hospital infrastructure. He possesses his black communications device with frozen Ministry access, technical knowledge, maintenance cable, forged slate, false authorization using Minister Rusk’s name, and maintenance coat. He is shaken, ashamed, resourceful, and committed to helping Mara despite losing institutional protection.
Mara confronted Administrator Halden with evidence of withheld Lumenex and falsified public health reports; Halden reported the confrontation to the Council instead of providing treatment.
The Council seized Eli from the family apartment and transferred him to the North Research Ward as a respiratory trial candidate under an emergency medical classification.
Sela resisted Eli’s seizure and was arrested for interfering with the medical transfer and attempting to obtain unauthorized treatment.
The Council sealed the Venn apartment, suspended household property access, and froze the family’s citizenship credits.
Tomas’s Ministry credentials were revoked or frozen during the seizure, demonstrating that his family’s influence could not protect him from Council retaliation.
Tomas forged a temporary hospital maintenance authorization using Minister Rusk’s name, granting Mara and himself twelve minutes of access to the restricted ward.
Mara and Tomas entered the hospital service spine in maintenance disguises and began descending toward the restricted levels to find Sela and Eli.
Mara and Tomas must use the forged hospital maintenance authorization to reach the restricted ward, rescue Sela and Eli, and escape through Lumen’s external service infrastructure.
The Council will investigate Tomas’s forged authorization and Minister Rusk’s apparent sponsorship, increasing the danger of detection.

chapters.name: The Descent Capsule
chapters.content:
The hospital service spine descended through the city like a throat swallowing them.

Mara kept one hand on the rail and the other around Tomas’s forged slate. Blue maintenance lights passed overhead at regular intervals, turning his face pale, then black, then pale again. Behind them, somewhere above the sealed family rings, the false authorization was already becoming a question in a Council office.

“Twelve minutes,” Tomas said.

“You said that two minutes ago.”

“I’m reminding myself.”

“You should remind the doors.”

At the next junction, a scanner unfolded from the wall. Tomas pressed the slate against it. The machine hesitated. Its lens narrowed, searching the authorization for a sponsor who existed only as a name borrowed from a man who would soon know it had been used.

Mara heard footsteps above them.

“Open,” she whispered.

The scanner flashed amber.

Tomas bent close to it. “Emergency filtration fault, North Research Ward. Pressure variance—”

“I know what the order says.”

“Then stop breathing like you’re going to faint.”

“I’m not.”

The door opened.

They slipped through as a pair of hospital technicians came down the upper stairwell. The door sealed behind them, muting the footsteps. For several seconds neither of them moved. The corridor beyond was narrower, crowded with warm pipes and cables wrapped in numbered sleeves. The air tasted metallic.

Mara checked the route on her drafting folio. “Ward level three is ahead. The transport holding area is below the clinical floors. If Sela was detained as a guardian, she’ll be in temporary custody, not the security cells.”

“How do you know?”

“I mapped the hospital’s waste and supply routes last year.”

“You mapped a prison without knowing it was a prison.”

“I mapped doors.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“It is when someone is trying to get through one.”

The corridor ended at a pressure door. A small window showed a room lined with restraint benches. Two empty cups sat on the floor. A woman in a gray detention wrap was slumped against the far wall, her hands bound in front of her.

“Mum.”

Mara struck the door release. Nothing happened.

Tomas scanned the slate. “This authorization covers medical maintenance, not custody.”

“Extend it.”

“I told you—”

“Extend it.”

He pulled the black communications device from his coat. Its screen still displayed the dead Ministry seal, but beneath it ran old maintenance protocols. Tomas attached the cable to the device and opened the service panel beside the door.

“Your route map,” he said.

“What about it?”

“Does this holding area have an independent lock?”

“Probably.”

“That’s not useful.”

“Look for a manual override on the east wall. Hospitals always have one. People panic when automatic doors fail.”

Tomas followed the cable behind the panel. “You say that as if you’ve seen it happen.”

“I’ve seen people panic when anything fails.”

A red indicator began pulsing beside the lock. Mara looked through the window again. Sela had lifted her head. For an instant their eyes met.

Sela rose too quickly and had to catch herself against the wall.

“Mum, it’s me.”

Sela crossed the room, pressing her bound hands to the glass. Her lips formed Mara’s name, but the door was insulated against sound.

Tomas twisted two wires together. Sparks jumped. The red indicator turned white.

“Now,” he said.

Mara found the override beneath a hinged plate and pulled it down. The door gave a heavy mechanical sigh. Sela stumbled through, and Mara caught her.

“You came,” Sela said.

“Of course I came.”

“Where is Eli?”

Mara’s arms tightened around her. “We’re going to him.”

Sela looked from Mara to Tomas. Recognition hardened her face. “You’re Minister Rusk’s son.”

“Tomas.”

“I know who you are.”

“He’s helping us,” Mara said.

“Then he can help us faster.”

Tomas held up the black transfer key. “The restraint release is coded to the custody registry. I can’t access it with my credentials frozen.”

Sela gave a short, humorless laugh. “They took the key from me when they arrested me.”

Mara felt the weight of the key in Tomas’s hand. “You have it.”

“I took it back.”

“From whom?”

“A guard who believed a mother was too frightened to notice his hands.”

Sela’s wrists were bruised where the binding had cut her. Mara touched one mark, then drew her fingers away.

“We have to find Eli.”

“I know.” Sela’s voice was low. “But listen to me, Mara. If they move us again, you take the files and leave.”

“No.”

“You take the files.”

“I’m not leaving you in here.”

“You already left him once.”

The words landed between them. Sela’s expression changed at once—not apology, exactly, but pain at having used the truth as a weapon.

Mara looked toward the ward doors. “I tried to stop them.”

“I know. I saw you.”

“Then don’t ask me to do it again.”

“I’m asking you to survive if they make you.”

A chime sounded through the service corridor.

Tomas checked the slate. “Nine minutes.”

“Eli is in the research ward,” Mara said. “We go there.”
