chapters.name: Return to Lumen
chapters.content:
The green indicator was not a light so much as a stubborn ember behind a pane of mineral glass. It blinked twice, paused, and blinked again.

Imani lifted one gloved hand. They stopped in the black water.

Mara heard only the rasp of her own breath and the small mechanical clicks of the filters. The tunnel had narrowed around them. Mud pressed against one wall, while the other disappeared into a shaft crowded with cables. Above, beyond layers of drowned masonry and the city’s foundations, Lumen waited.

Nia held the lamp close to her chest. “Signal?”

“Old maintenance marker,” Imani whispered. “The intake junction is ahead.”

“Or a lure,” Tomas said.

“Everything is a lure if you are frightened enough.”

“I am frightened enough.”

Mara looked back at him. His face was pale behind the mask, his bruised ribs making each breath shallow. “Good. Frightened people check their footing.”

“Comforting.”

They moved on.

The tunnel rose gradually, and the water fell from their waists to their knees. At the junction, Imani found a manual wheel beneath the silt. Nia cleared it with both hands, sending brown clouds through the lamps. Tomas unfolded the access slate inside its waterproof sleeve and pressed the forged authorization against a reader that had no visible power.

For several seconds nothing happened.

Then the reader woke.

A line of amber text appeared: MAINTENANCE SPINE 4—DECOMMISSIONED.

Tomas exhaled. “It believes us.”

“No,” Mara said. “It believes the dead.”

The wheel turned with a groan. Somewhere overhead, a lock released. The floor shuddered, and a vertical shaft opened in the wall, revealing a ladder disappearing into darkness.

Imani climbed first. Nia followed with the cable coil over one shoulder. Mara went next, the waterproof map sealed against her chest. Every rung was slick. Twice her injured leg slipped, and each time Tomas’s hand caught the back of her harness before she fell.

At the top, they entered a chamber no larger than a freight lift. Its walls were tiled in the white ceramic Lumen used before the city’s lower rings had begun to peel and stain. A service hatch waited above them.

Imani placed her ear against it.

“What do you hear?” Mara asked.

“Fans. One working, one failing.”

Nia smiled without humor. “Welcome home.”

Imani opened the hatch.

Warm air spilled down the shaft, carrying the smells of oil, citrus disinfectant, and the faint metallic sweetness of recycled rain. Mara climbed through and found herself in a maintenance corridor beneath Lumen’s eastern transit ring.

For a moment, she could not move.

The city was still there.

A strip of blue light ran along the corridor floor. Somewhere beyond the bulkhead, a familiar three-note chime sounded, followed by the soft voice of the transit system announcing a delay on the North-South loop. The music was the same one Mara had heard every morning since childhood: bright, descending notes meant to make waiting feel orderly.

She had expected alarms, empty halls, perhaps the raw exposed machinery of a city already dying. Instead, a cleaner’s cart stood beside the wall. Someone had left a paper cup on it, folded around a sprig of mint.

Tomas came up behind her. He looked toward the chime.

“I used to hate that announcement,” he said.

“You still can.”

“I think I miss it.”

That frightened her more than the tunnel had. Missing a sound did not mean forgiving the system that made it. It meant the system had wrapped itself around the ordinary parts of a life.

Imani shut the hatch. “Change clothes.”

They opened the equipment cases. The mainland clothing vanished beneath gray maintenance coveralls taken from a sealed emergency locker. Imani cut the settlement insignia from their sleeves. Nia tucked her hair beneath a service cap and clipped a tool harness around her waist. Tomas put on a respirator mask with a cracked Ministry seal, then hid his forged access slate in the inner pocket of his coat.

Mara exchanged her damp trousers for work pants and fastened a badge to her chest. The badge belonged to a maintenance worker who had died nine years earlier. His name was Halen Quist.

“Try not to answer to Halen,” Tomas said.

“I will answer to Mara.”

“Not loudly.”

They stepped into the service corridor.

The first checkpoint came after three turns. Two security officers stood beneath a camera, examining a queue of workers whose shift permits had been flagged. Their uniforms were clean, but one officer’s left sleeve had been repaired with blue thread. Mara remembered seeing that thread in the lower rings. Even security officers were patching their clothes now.

Imani pushed a cart of filters toward the checkpoint. Mara walked beside it, carrying a diagnostic case. Nia kept her head down. Tomas took the rear.

“Maintenance team,” the nearer officer called. “Ring designation?”

“Eastern transit filtration,” Mara answered.

The officer scanned her badge. The reader flashed yellow.

“Your route is not on the current schedule.”

“It is on the emergency schedule,” Mara said. “Filter differential rose in the lower intake. If you want the ring closed, call your supervisor and explain why you delayed a pressure repair.”

The officer’s expression hardened. “You have a great deal to say for a filter worker.”

Mara felt Tomas tense behind her.

Before the officer could ask another question, a woman in a green Ministry jacket came striding from the opposite corridor. She carried a stack of broadcast folders against her chest and looked furious.

“Are you stopping the eastern repair again?” she demanded. “The Ministry has already filed two complaints about your delays.”

The officer turned. “We have a badge discrepancy.”

“Then record it and let them pass. If the transit loop fails during the ministerial rehearsal, I will put your name on the incident report.”

The officer glanced at the camera, then waved them through.

Mara did not look at the woman until they reached the next junction. The woman kept walking, not once acknowledging them.

Tomas murmured, “Jori Pell.”

“Your colleague?”

“Former colleague. Broadcast traffic analysis.”

“Why did she help?”

“Because she knows what a failed transit loop does to a hospital.”

“Or because she knows you.”

“Both can be true.”

The corridor opened onto the eastern market ring. Mara stopped again.

Crowds moved beneath a ceiling of artificial blue. Vendors shouted over one another from stalls built into old maintenance alcoves. There were baskets of mushrooms, printed meal sheets, recycled fabric, copper fasteners, bright candies made from algae sugar. A boy in a school jacket argued with his sister over a mechanical bird whose wings had been repaired with foil.

Beyond the market, gardens glowed in tiers beneath lamps tuned to a permanent spring. Vines climbed trellises. Dwarf pear trees held pale fruit. School groups passed in orderly lines, their teachers tapping attendance tablets while children stared at a display of preserved surface fossils.

Mara knew the market’s geometry: three exits, two concealed supply lifts, one public clinic, one water station. She knew where the Council’s cameras hung and which stalls received upper-ring allocations. She had drawn these spaces as colored blocks on maps that reduced people to flow rates.

Now an old woman was bargaining over onions. A maintenance apprentice was asleep against a crate. Two workers shared a cup of tea beneath a sign announcing the Crown Seal celebration in twelve days.

Twelve days.

Mara’s stomach tightened.

The celebration banners hung above the crowd: LUMEN SECURE. LUMEN ETERNAL. Under them, families bought festival ribbons and children practiced a song about the city rising above a poisoned world.

“Do not stare,” Imani said.

“I know these people.”

“You know the city’s idea of them.”

“No.” Mara watched a mother wipe sauce from her daughter’s mouth. “I know that mother. I know that child.”

Imani’s voice softened. “Then remember them when the systems fail.”

A public screen flickered above the market. Minister Rusk appeared, older than Mara remembered, his expression composed beneath the Crown Seal emblem.

“Preparations continue,” he said. “Lumen remains protected by the vigilance of its citizens. Report unauthorized contact, foreign intrusion, and the circulation of destabilizing material.”

The screen shifted to an image of the mainland: gray water, a burned tower, a skeletal tree.

A man at the onion stall spat on the floor. “Always the same picture.”

The vendor beside him lowered her voice. “Keep it down.”

“Why? They can hear us whether we talk or not.”

The woman looked toward a camera and pulled her child closer.

Mara felt the truth settle differently inside her. Fear was not agreement. Silence was not loyalty. The city had trained people to protect themselves first, and then called that obedience.

They reached the abandoned relay office through a locked storeroom behind the market’s water station. Jori Pell was waiting inside with three other Ministry workers. One was a signal technician Mara recognized from broadcasts; another had served refreshments during Council briefings. The third kept watch at the door, trembling so hard that the keys on his belt chimed.

“We can give you nine minutes on the emergency channel,” Jori said. “Not now. The Ministry is monitoring all central traffic. But we can route a maintenance diagnostic through the old rehearsal studio.”

Tomas looked at the others. “Why help us?”

The signal technician rubbed his eyes. “Because I have spent six years cutting the sound from people’s pleas before they reached the city.”

The trembling man said, “Because my daughter is in the lower respiratory ward.”

Jori’s gaze sharpened. “And because if we do nothing, the Crown Seal will be activated by people who have already decided which of us can be lost.”

Tomas nodded once. “We need hospital transfer schedules. Eli Venn. Sela Venn.”

Jori’s face changed at Sela’s name.

“Sela was released from the holding system,” she said. “The Ministry marked her for compulsory filtration labor in Ring Eight. But the last location field is blank.”

“Blank how?” Mara asked.

“Not missing. Suppressed.”

“By whom?”

“Someone with administrative clearance.”

Tomas stepped closer. “And Eli?”

“North Atmospheric Research Hospital. Transfer order scheduled for tomorrow at 04:10.”

“Transfer where?”

Jori hesitated. “The order says central tower evaluation.”

Imani swore under her breath.

Mara imagined Eli being moved through the city while asleep, his lungs tethered to a machine, his name reduced to a code on a cart. “Can you stop it?”

“No. But I can tell you which lift they will use.” Jori pulled a paper map from her folder. “The central systems are watching digital requests. Use paper. Use people.”

Nia spread the map across a workbench. “Where are the filters?”

Jori blinked. “What?”

“Resource stores. Oxygen, masks, water, medical supplies. If the Crown Seal starts or the Council locks the rings, people will need them.”

Mara took a grease pencil from her case.

The map was official, clean, and almost useless. It showed districts, transit lines, and approved clinics. It did not show the emergency oxygen lockers behind the market, the water reserve beneath the school gardens, or the service lift that connected them. Mara added each location in a thin red line.

“Here,” she said. “Ring Eight has a filter depot under the old tram platform. Ring Six has a clinic supply store accessed through the laundry maintenance shaft. This garden has a backup water tank.”

Jori stared. “Those are restricted locations.”

“They are resources.”

Tomas watched the pencil move. “If the map reaches the wrong people—”

“It will,” Mara said. “Every map reaches the wrong people eventually.”

She drew alternate routes around the checkpoints, marked doors that could be opened manually, and added the names of workers who might help. She left out no citizenship tier. Beside each resource she wrote: OPEN IF NEEDED. VERIFY WITH TWO WITNESSES.

The signal technician leaned over the table. “You are making a public distribution map.”

“I am making a map people can use when the official one becomes a lie.”

A sharp alarm sounded outside.

The watchman at the door went white. “Someone reported the maintenance team.”

Jori gathered the paper map and shoved it beneath a stack of blank Ministry forms. “There are security officers coming from the market.”

Imani closed the equipment case. “Which way?”

Mara looked at the corridor plan, then at the map she had just altered. The old routes rose in her mind: service stairs, garden access, a sealed tram platform, the hidden supply line she had once copied for herself.

“Not the eastern exit,” she said. “They will expect us there.”

She circled a narrow passage beneath the school garden.

“It leads to Ring Eight,” Tomas said.

“It leads to people,” Mara replied. “And to the filtration labor block. If Sela’s location was suppressed, someone may be hiding her there—or hiding what happened to her.”

Jori caught her wrist. “If you are caught, they will call you a terrorist.”

Mara looked through the wall toward the market, where the transit music had begun again and children were singing beneath the celebration banners.

“They already called the mainland dead,” she said. “They are not reliable judges of reality.”

The door shuddered under a fist.

Jori lifted the stack of forms. “Go.”

They slipped through the garden passage as security entered the relay office. Mara led them down a stairwell between glowing vines and humming water pipes. The city’s artificial sunlight warmed her face. For one impossible second, she could pretend she had only come home late from work.

Then the alarm spread through the ring, and every lamp turned red.

Mara unfolded a blank sheet over her knee while they ran. With the grease pencil, she began again: not the city as the Council had drawn it, but the city as it might survive. A route to oxygen. A route to water. A route to the hospital. A route for strangers to find one another.

At the bottom she wrote the first instruction.

NO ONE RESOURCE BELONGS TO ONE TIER.

Then she marked the path toward Ring Eight, where Sela might be waiting and where, before dawn, Eli would be moved.

chapters.name: The Lower Rings
chapters.content:
The stairwell ended behind a wall of dead ivy.

Mara pressed her shoulder against the service panel, and it opened with a sigh. Warm, sour air rolled over them. Ring Eight lay beyond: a residential level built around the oldest buoyancy supports, where the ceilings were low and the lamps had the tired yellow cast of old teeth.

Nia came through after her and looked up at the vents. “That fan is running backward.”

“How can you tell?” Tomas whispered.

“Because it is blowing dust into my eyes.”

Imani eased the panel shut. Behind them, security voices echoed faintly through the garden passage. Mara tucked the grease pencil into her sleeve and lifted the paper map Jori had given them. The official route showed a broad corridor from the school gardens to the Ring Eight filtration block. The corridor in front of them had been narrowed by stacked ration crates and a line of people waiting beside a water tap.

No one in the queue spoke. Their faces had the blank concentration of people saving breath.

A woman held a metal cup under the tap. Brown water struck the bottom, paused, then came in a thin clear thread. She filled the cup and passed it to a child. The child drank. The woman did not.

Mara felt the old reflex rise in her: record the delay, calculate the pressure, report the irregularity. It was the same reflex that had once made suffering look like a system problem instead of a person’s thirst.

Nia stepped toward the tap.

The woman’s hand closed around the cup. “No trouble.”

“We are not trouble,” Nia said. “We are maintenance.”

“Maintenance is trouble when it arrives with a Council badge.”

Mara touched her own badge. “It is a dead worker’s badge.”

The woman studied her. “That makes it worse.”

A man near the back of the queue coughed into a rag. Several people turned away from him. Above them, a public screen displayed a blue-and-gold animation of Lumen’s upper districts: towers washed in clean light, gardens spilling over terraces, children running beneath a banner that read TWELVE DAYS TO THE CROWN SEAL.

A voice announced, “Celebration ration supplements are now available to certified households in Rings One through Three. Lower-ring allocations remain stable through the transition period.”

Someone laughed.

It was not a happy sound. “Stable,” the man with the rag said. “That means smaller.”

The screen changed to a menu of celebration foods: citrus paste, pressed grain cakes, preserved fish. At the bottom, in small lettering, appeared the ordinary allocation. It had fallen again.

Mara took out her notebook. “How long has the water been discolored?”

The woman’s expression sharpened. “Why?”

“Because the intake filter may be failing. If we know when it began, we can identify which membrane is damaged.”

“And then?”

“Then we repair it.”

“Before or after the celebration?”

Mara had no answer that did not sound like a lie.

Nia looked at the tap housing. “The flow regulator is clogged. Not the membrane. Someone put a cloth in the intake.”

“Why would someone do that?” Tomas asked.

“To slow the flow,” Nia said. “If the pressure falls below the sensor threshold, the system reports a shortage. Then the Council sends less water and blames the ring.”

Imani’s face went still. “Can you clear it?”

Nia glanced at Mara. “If people move back.”

The queue did not move. But the woman with the cup stepped aside. One by one, the others followed, not obediently, but with the wary cooperation of people who had already decided the repair mattered more than the delay.

Nia knelt, opened her tool harness, and worked the housing loose. A strip of gray cloth emerged from the pipe, wound around a twist of wire. Someone had placed it carefully. The water ran faster.

A murmur passed through the queue.

“Who did that?” Tomas asked.

“No one who wants to be named,” the woman said.

Mara wrote: deliberate restriction at east tap; pressure manipulation; witnesses present. She hesitated, then wrote the woman’s name when the woman finally gave it: Amel Daro.

“Do not put that in a Council report,” Amel said.

“It is not a Council report.”

“Not yet.”

Mara closed the notebook. “If you keep a copy?”

Amel looked at the screen advertising citrus paste. “We have copies of many things.”

The sentence followed Mara as they moved deeper into the ring.

The filtration block occupied the central spine, behind a set of doors painted with the old Lumen emblem. The emblem had been scrubbed so often that the metal beneath it shone. A guard sat at a desk outside, reading a celebration bulletin. His mask hung below his chin.

Imani pushed the filter cart forward. “Emergency replacement membranes.”

The guard barely looked up. “Labor identification.”

Mara presented her badge. “Eastern transit filtration.”

“Not here. This is compulsory labor.”

“We have an equipment fault.”

“Then file a fault.”

“We are filing one now.”

His gaze moved over the four of them, lingered on Tomas’s posture, and stopped at Nia’s tool harness. “You have no labor assignment.”

Nia smiled. “I am very adaptable.”

The guard reached for the wall terminal. Imani moved first, leaning over the cart as if to retrieve a membrane. The cart’s side struck the desk. The terminal jolted loose from its bracket and went dark.

“Fault,” Imani said.

The guard stood. Nia stepped between him and the cart.

Mara heard footsteps inside the block. More than one person. She pushed open the labor door.

The filtration chamber was enormous and loud. Banks of cylindrical filters rose from the floor to the ceiling, connected by pipes that shook with every pulse. Workers in gray coveralls stood on platforms, stripping clogged membranes from the housings. Their faces were filmed with white mineral dust. Some wore Council respirators; most wore folded cloth over their mouths.

At the far end, a woman lifted a replacement panel with one arm while holding her injured shoulder against her body.

Mara knew the tilt of that head before the woman turned.

“Sela.”

Her mother froze.

For a moment, the chamber became soundless, though the machines continued pounding around them. Sela’s hair had been cut unevenly. A bruise yellowed along her jaw, and a strip of dressing showed beneath her collar. Her hands were red and cracked from chemical wash.

“Mara?”

Mara crossed the platform too quickly. Her injured leg gave way, and Sela caught her before she fell. The embrace was awkward between respirators and tool belts, but it was real. Sela’s body was thinner than it had been at Tilbury. She smelled of antiseptic, metal, and the soap used in the holding cells.

“You came back,” Sela said.

“I came for you.”

“You came for Eli.”

“For both of you.”

Sela held her at arm’s length. Her eyes traveled over Mara’s bruised shoulder, the cut on her leg, the maintenance badge. “You look terrible.”

“So do you.”

“That is a family tradition.”

Mara laughed once, and then she was crying. She pressed her forehead against Sela’s. Around them, the workers continued pretending not to watch.

Tomas stood at the edge of the platform. “Sela, we have to leave.”

Sela looked past Mara at him, then at Imani and Nia. “You brought the whole mainland into the filtration block?”

“Nia is from Tilbury,” Mara said. “Imani too.”

“I know where they are from.” Sela’s gaze rested on Tomas. “And you are still carrying trouble in your coat.”

“Several kinds,” Tomas said.

A warning tone sounded above the chamber. The filtration pressure had dropped again. Workers turned toward the main gauges. Three indicators had gone red.

Sela pulled Mara toward a control box. “They have been reducing the intake to the lower rings. The machines are being kept just above failure.”

“Why?”

“Because the upper districts need clean air for the celebration rehearsals. And because when we complain, they say the lower rings consume too much.”

Imani examined the gauge. “This differential cannot hold twelve days.”

“It does not have to,” Sela said. “They expect Crown Seal systems to take over before then.”

Mara looked at the workers. “How many know?”

“Everyone who has repaired a filter.”

“That is not enough.”

“No,” Sela said. “It is more than enough to make them afraid.”

She pointed to a stack of membrane panels. The panels were marked for Ring One. Beside them sat a smaller stack labeled RING EIGHT—DEFERRED.

Mara’s anger rose so quickly it made her dizzy. “They are sending the good membranes upward.”

“They are sending all the good things upward.”

Nia picked up one of the discarded panels. “These are not unusable. They need cleaning and a pressure reset.”

Sela’s mouth tightened. “We have been told not to touch them.”

“Who told you?”

“The labor supervisor.”

“Is he here?”

A broad-shouldered man on the lower platform raised his hand without turning around. “He is dead tired and has not been paid in nineteen days.”

Another worker called, “Twenty-one.”

“Twenty-one,” the man corrected.

The chamber changed. Workers began exchanging looks. A woman near the pressure manifold tapped two fingers against her wrist. Someone on the opposite platform answered with the same gesture.

Mara recognized no official signal. It was not a code from the Ministry or the cartography office. It was older, improvised, passed hand to hand.

Sela saw her notice. “They have been making lists.”

“Of what?”

“Filters that can be restored. Water points that still function. Children who need oxygen. Which guards will look away. Which doors have manual releases.”

“Who is coordinating it?”

“No one.” Sela glanced at the workers. “That is the point. If one person keeps the list, the Council has one person to arrest.”

A small woman at the manifold called, “We share the list by memory.”

“Memory loses details,” Mara said.

“So does a prison record,” the woman replied.

Mara thought of her map: OPEN IF NEEDED. VERIFY WITH TWO WITNESSES. She pulled it from inside her coverall and spread it on the control box. Sela bent over the paper. Nia drew the filtration block’s actual pipe routes, while Imani marked pressure gates and emergency bypasses. Workers added names and warnings in the margins.

A guard entered the chamber.

“Back to assigned positions,” he shouted. “Unauthorized gathering is a civic violation.”

Nobody moved.

Mara felt the silence gather, not as courage exactly, but as a decision to stop making the guard’s work easy. The broad-shouldered worker lowered his wrench. The woman at the manifold turned off her station light. One by one, the chamber’s platforms darkened until the guard stood under a single failing lamp.

Sela whispered, “Now.”

Nia and Imani crossed to the deferred membrane stack. Tomas blocked the doorway, speaking rapidly into his hidden slate, perhaps recording, perhaps sending a message through one of Jori’s channels. Mara helped Sela lift a panel into the housing.

The guard reached for his alarm.

A worker behind him shut the door.

“Do not,” Sela said.

The guard looked from the workers to the dark platforms. His hand fell away.

They worked for six minutes. Nia cleaned the membrane, Imani reset the pressure valve, and Mara followed the old route markings through the service panels. When the final clamp locked, the filters roared. Air moved through the chamber with a deep, rising breath.

The red gauges turned amber.

Then one turned green.

No one cheered. The people in Ring Eight had learned not to celebrate too soon. But the woman at the manifold began to cry, and the broad-shouldered worker rested both hands on his wrench as if it were a staff.

Sela closed the panel. “You cannot stay here.”

“I am not leaving you.”

“You are leaving me to go after Eli.”

“His transfer is at 04:10.”

Sela’s face changed. “Tomorrow?”

Mara nodded. “Central tower evaluation. The research hospital moved him.”

For one instant, Sela’s hands shook. Then she gripped the edge of the control box until they steadied.

“Can we reach him?”

“We know the lift route,” Tomas said. “We have help in the Ministry. We have nine minutes on an emergency channel, maybe more if we can keep the system confused.”

“And after you expose everything?” Sela asked.

Mara met her eyes. “People deserve to know.”

“Yes.” Sela looked toward the breathing filters. “But truth does not open a stuck valve. It does not keep a crowd from tearing apart a ration store. If you tell them the city is built on their suffering, some will help you. Some will decide that anyone who knew must be punished. Some will destroy the machines because they think the machines are the enemy.”

“I know.”

“No, you know it as a plan. I know it as a mother.” Sela touched Mara’s cheek. “When the descent begins, people will be terrified. They may do terrible things to survive. Do not give them only the truth. Give them routes. Give them names. Give them someone to ask what happens next.”

Mara glanced at the map crowded with handwriting.

“I am trying.”

“Try harder than the Council did.”

Mara flinched. Sela saw it and softened.

“I am not blaming you for leaving,” she said. “You left because we told you to live. You found the mainland because you were brave enough to believe what you saw. But bravery is not permission to make other people into sacrifices.”

“I would never—”

“I know.” Sela pressed her forehead to Mara’s. “That is why I am telling you.”

The emergency tone sounded again, this time from the corridor. Security had found the block.

Sela tore a strip from her labor sleeve and wrapped it around Mara’s injured leg, tightening the cloth above the cut. “There is a laundry shaft behind the old reserve tank. It reaches Ring Seven, then the hospital service line.”

“You are coming.”

“I have work.”

“Mum.”

“If I leave now, they will shut the filters again. These people need someone who knows which valves still answer.”

Mara wanted to argue. She wanted to drag Sela through the door and keep her where no system could reach her. But the workers were already gathering around the map, copying routes onto scraps of packaging, memorizing the locations of oxygen stores and manual releases.

Sela was not trapped in the labor block in the way Mara had imagined. She was trapped, yes—but she was also making the trap less powerful for everyone inside it.

Mara folded the map and handed Sela a copy. “Keep this hidden.”

Sela tucked it beneath her coverall. “You keep one too.”

“I have three.”

“Then you are learning.”

Nia opened the reserve-tank hatch. Tomas checked the corridor. Imani placed one hand on Sela’s shoulder.

“We will return,” Imani said.

Sela gave her a tired smile. “Return with my son.”

“We will.”

Sela looked at Mara. “Do not promise what you cannot control.”

Mara swallowed. “We will do everything we can to bring him back.”

“That I can believe.”

Mara descended into the shaft. Before the hatch closed, she looked up once more. Sela stood among the workers beneath the failing lamps, one hand on the restored filter and the other over the hidden map.

The lower rings were not waiting to be saved. They were already saving one another in fragments: a cloth removed from a water intake, a membrane cleaned instead of discarded, a list carried in memory, a door held shut against an alarm.

Mara climbed after Nia toward the hospital route. Above them, the celebration announcement began again, promising security, eternity, and a city without fear.

Below it, through the pipes and walls, the lower rings passed along a different message.

Water here.

Air here.

Someone is watching the door.

Someone is coming.

And when Mara reached the next junction, she added the words to her map—not as a slogan, but as an instruction people could use.

FIND ONE ANOTHER.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old former Lumen apprentice cartographer, currently leaving Ring Eight through an old reserve-tank laundry shaft toward Ring Seven and the hospital service line with Nia, Tomas, and Imani. Her bruised shoulder and cut leg ache but remain functional; Sela tightened a cloth bandage around the leg. Mara carries her waterproof route map, notebook, drafting tools, collaborative relay maps, recorder, grease pencil, forged maintenance identification, and an expanding illegal public-use survival map now marked with oxygen, water, repair, safe-door, and hospital routes. She has reunited with Sela, learned that Sela is staying in Ring Eight to maintain restored filters, and learned that Eli was moved to central tower evaluation with transfer scheduled for 04:10. She now understands that lower-ring workers are already organizing through decentralized resource and repair networks, and that truth must be broadcast alongside practical survival guidance. Her immediate goals are to reach the hospital route, rescue Eli and other patients, support the broadcast and controlled Crown Seal conversion, protect civilians, and distribute usable maps. She is emotionally relieved but frightened after seeing Sela, accepts Sela’s warning about unintended chaos, and remains partnered with Tomas, Imani, and Nia.

set.name: Sela Venn
set.description: Mara and Eli’s mother, currently remaining in Ring Eight’s filtration labor block under compulsory unpaid labor and threat of losing housing. She is exhausted, underfed, and marked by a healing forehead wound, bruised wrists, injured shoulder, cracked chemical-burned hands, and a yellowing jaw bruise, but is alert, protective, practical, and organizing workers. She reunited with Mara and helped restore a deferred filtration membrane, then concealed a copy of Mara’s survival map among the workers’ decentralized lists. She knows Eli has been moved to central tower evaluation and that Mara’s group is pursuing the hospital service line. She refuses to blame Mara for leaving and supports exposing the truth, but warns that revelation without routes, names, resources, and guidance could make Lumen’s descent chaotic and deadly. Her immediate goal is to keep Ring Eight’s filters functioning and strengthen the worker network while Mara rescues Eli. She remains allied with Imani and the mainland network and deeply bonded to Mara and Eli.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Twelve-year-old respiratory trial candidate alive in Council custody, moved from North Atmospheric Research Hospital toward central tower evaluation with transfer scheduled for 04:10 the next day. He remains dependent on continuous respiratory support after a dangerous atmospheric exposure trial and does not know the full rescue plan. Mara and Sela now know the transfer timing and have a route toward the hospital service line. His immediate need remains stabilization with the mainland treatment and rescue before further experimentation or transfer worsens his condition.

set.name: Tomas Rusk
set.description: Junior communications aide and Minister Rusk’s son, currently disguised as a maintenance worker and leaving Ring Eight through the old reserve-tank laundry shaft with Mara, Nia, and Imani. His bruised ribs remain painful, and he is tired, frightened, and focused on accountability rather than family loyalty or vengeance. He carries the forged access slate sealed inside his coat and retains Ministry authorization patterns, emergency channels, encrypted traffic, hospital transfer data, and relay coordination knowledge. He helped secure the known 04:10 transfer information and is attempting to use Jori Pell’s nine-minute emergency-channel window while supporting the broadcast and hospital rescue. He witnessed the lower-ring workers’ decentralized resistance and understands that practical guidance is essential during conversion. He has a complicated bond with Mara, respects Imani’s caution, trusts Nia’s technical judgment, and remains committed to preventing civilian deaths.

set.name: Imani Okafor
set.description: Former Lumen atmospheric engineer, currently disguised as a maintenance worker and moving with Mara, Tomas, and Nia from Ring Eight through the old reserve-tank laundry shaft toward Ring Seven and the hospital service line. She is tense, vigilant, and physically tired, carrying technical knowledge of pressure gates, filtration systems, relay timing, and the controlled-conversion design, along with maintenance equipment and relay materials. She helped diagnose and reset Ring Eight’s deferred membrane, witnessed the workers’ decentralized resistance, and understands Sela’s choice to remain behind to keep the filters operating. Her goals are to guide the hospital infiltration, protect civilians and patients, and convert the closed Crown Seal feedback loop without sacrificing Lumen or the mainland. She conditionally trusts Mara and Tomas, respects Nia’s practical skill, and remains committed to distributed rather than centralized control.

set.name: Nia Vale
set.description: Seventeen-year-old mainland boat mechanic, currently disguised as a maintenance worker and descending with Mara, Tomas, and Imani through the old reserve-tank laundry shaft toward Ring Seven and the hospital service line. She is blunt, capable, alert, and determined to be treated as a responsible mechanic. She identified deliberate pressure manipulation at Ring Eight’s water tap, cleared the obstruction, cleaned a deferred filtration membrane, and helped reset its pressure valve, earning practical trust from the workers. She carries her tool harness and knows improvised systems, scavenged couplings, damaged infrastructure, and second-reading safety practices better than formal manuals. Her immediate goals are to support the hospital rescue, repair machinery during controlled conversion, and keep the group moving through failing infrastructure. She has mutual respect with Mara, a challenging but accepted working relationship with Imani, and technical trust with Tomas.
Mara reunited with Sela in Ring Eight’s compulsory filtration block and learned that Sela is being forced into unpaid labor under threat of losing housing.
Mara, Sela, Nia, Imani, and Ring Eight workers restored a deferred filtration membrane, improving the ring’s failing air supply and demonstrating coordinated resistance.

Sela warned Mara that exposing the Council’s crimes without practical routes, resources, and guidance could make Lumen’s descent chaotic and deadly; she urged Mara to pair truth with survival instructions.
Ring Eight workers revealed a decentralized resistance network sharing resource lists, repair knowledge, safe doors, oxygen needs, and guard patterns without relying on a single coordinator.

Sela gave Mara a hidden route through the old reserve-tank laundry shaft toward Ring Seven and the hospital service line, while remaining in Ring Eight to maintain the restored filters and support workers.

chapters.name: The Father’s Secret
chapters.content:
The laundry shaft opened into a service corridor beneath Ring Seven, where the walls sweated condensation and the lights came on only after they had passed. Nia went first, carrying the tool harness against her chest. Imani followed with the relay case. Mara kept one hand on the wall and the other on her map, while Tomas brought up the rear, listening to the faint pulse of Ministry traffic through the forged slate inside his coat.

At the junction, three arrows had been drawn in grease pencil.

HOSPITAL—left.
MINISTRY—up.
NO RETURN—down.

Tomas stopped beneath them. “I need to go up.”

Mara turned. “You need to come with us.”

“If I do, we reach the service line without the emergency codes. If I go to the Ministry, I may get Eli’s exact ward, the transfer authorization, and the channel key.”

“May?”

“My father keeps the inner broadcast registers.”

Imani studied the corridor above. “And if he recognizes you?”

“He will recognize me.”

“That was not my question.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened. “He may let me in because he still believes I can be corrected.”

Nia looked at the arrow marked NO RETURN. “That sounds encouraging.”

“It is not.” Tomas removed the forged slate from his coat. Its screen showed a maintenance request authorized by a name that no longer had authority to authorize anything. “The Ministry’s central tower is sealed to everyone below Ministerial clearance. My father can open the inner lift. He can also summon every guard in the building.”

Mara’s shoulder throbbed beneath the borrowed uniform. She thought of Sela standing among the filter workers, refusing rescue because other people needed the air. She thought of Eli’s scheduled transfer, a time printed in a file as if a child’s life were a shipment.

“How long?” she asked.

“Nine minutes on the emergency channel, if Jori’s people can keep the loop alive. I need to reach my father before the window begins.”

“And if he refuses?”

“Then I come back.”

Imani’s gaze sharpened. “With what?”

Tomas looked at Mara. “With whatever I learn.”

Mara wanted to say that knowledge was not enough. She had spent months learning the difference between a map and a route, between a fact and a way to survive it. But Tomas was already taking off his maintenance cap.

“Do not go alone,” Nia said.

“I am going to my father’s office. Alone is the safest disguise.”

“You are going to a man who commands a ministry,” Imani said. “That is not a disguise. That is a negotiation.”

Tomas gave a humorless smile. “In my family, we call it dinner.”

Mara caught his sleeve before he could climb the stairs. “Bring back Eli’s location. And the codes.”

His eyes held hers. “I will try.”

“Do not promise what you cannot control.”

The words were Sela’s, but Tomas heard them as a warning. He nodded once and disappeared upward.

Mara watched until the lights swallowed him.

The Broadcast Ministry occupied the central tower above the city’s oldest transit ring. Its lower floors held studios, editing rooms, and banks of transmission equipment. Its upper floors were reserved for policy, strategy, and the private offices of people whose voices could turn a shortage into an act of nature.

Tomas entered through the maintenance lift with his identification turned face-down. At the fourth security gate, the guard glanced at the slate and then at Tomas’s face.

“Rusk?”

“Communications systems audit.”

“You are not cleared for this level.”

“The audit is for the level above.”

The guard frowned at the authorization. Tomas let irritation enter his posture, the familiar irritation of a privileged son inconvenienced by procedure. It worked. The guard swiped him through.

The Ministry smelled of hot circuitry and polished stone. On the public floors, technicians hurried between consoles while screens displayed the same blue-and-gold city that had watched Mara’s family go hungry. A caption rolled beneath it:

CONTINUITY IS SAFETY.

Tomas passed a studio where an announcer rehearsed the Crown Seal celebration address.

“Lumen endures because Lumen remains united,” the announcer said. “Outside the enclosure lies instability, violence, and—”

The studio door closed before Tomas heard the rest.

His father’s office was at the top of the administrative wing. The lock recognized Tomas’s face after a delay long enough to feel like an accusation.

Minister Rusk stood beside the window, looking down through the cloud glass. Lumen’s lower rings were hidden in shadow. Above them, the upper towers shone beneath artificial dawn.

“You are alive,” Rusk said.

Tomas entered and let the door seal behind him. “You sound disappointed.”

“I sound relieved.”

“You reported me as an accomplice to domestic terrorism.”

“I reported that you were compromised.”

“Is that what you call it?”

Rusk turned. He was older than Tomas remembered from broadcasts, his hair silver at the temples, his collar unfastened. Without the cameras, his authority looked less like strength than exhaustion carefully maintained.

“You came here because you need something,” he said.

“I need Eli Venn’s location.”

The minister’s expression barely moved. “The boy is a classified medical subject.”

“He is twelve.”

“He is unstable and uniquely responsive to atmospheric exposure.”

“He is being used because his family is low-tier and cannot stop you.”

Rusk walked to his desk. “You have been listening to mainland agitators.”

“I have been listening to doctors. Engineers. People whose names you erased.”

“People who survived by scavenging the ruins we protected them from.”

Tomas placed both hands on the desk. “They have clinics, schools, gardens, power cooperatives. They know exactly what our systems are doing to them.”

“And they know that Lumen contains the only stable atmospheric technology left on the planet.” Rusk’s voice hardened. “If we open the city, every faction below will demand access. They will seize the arrays, dismantle the stabilizers, and bring the entire structure down. Millions may die.”

“Millions are already paying for it.”

“Not people you have met.”

Tomas felt the words strike more deeply than he expected. His father had always spoken as though distance were proof of wisdom. Tomas thought of Tilbury’s children, of the rashes on their hands and the careful way they breathed.

“I have met them,” he said. “That is why I am here.”

Rusk looked toward the window. “Secrecy protected humanity from panic.”

“No. Secrecy protected the Council from accountability.”

For the first time, anger broke through his father’s composure. “You think truth is a medicine? You release one image of a mainland garden and the lower rings riot. You tell them the air is poisoned and they tear open the filters. You tell them the city can descend and they rush the platforms. Panic kills faster than toxins.”

“Then give them instructions.”

“Instructions require authority.”

“Authority is what caused this.”

Rusk laughed once, without amusement. “You sound like your mother.”

Tomas went still.

The minister opened a drawer and removed a thin black file. It was not marked with a classification stripe. It had no title, only a date from fourteen years earlier.

“Why are you showing me that?” Tomas asked.

“Because you came here believing this was a simple contest between truth and lies.” Rusk rested his hand on the file. “It is not simple.”

He opened it.

The first page contained a maintenance report from Array T-17. The second bore a name Tomas knew from Mara’s family records.

DARIAN VENN.

Tomas read the line twice. “Mara’s father.”

“Your father’s colleague,” Rusk said. “Before he became your friend’s father.”

“What happened?”

Rusk’s eyes lowered. “Darian discovered that the early arrays were redirecting emissions toward the mainland. He believed the containment model was being falsified. He tried to transmit the data to the public network.”

“Why did no one tell us?”

“Because he was stopped.”

Tomas turned the page. There was a security incident report, a photograph of a maintenance platform, and a death certificate that named equipment failure as the cause. Beneath it, stamped in red, was a handwritten correction.

SUBJECT REMOVED AFTER SABOTAGE ATTEMPT. WITNESS EXPOSURE: TWO TECHNICIANS. PUBLIC ACCOUNT: ACCIDENT.

Tomas could not breathe.

“My father knew?”

“I knew.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Rusk did not answer immediately. “Your father knew enough to understand what would happen if the Council lost control of the city.”

“Did he kill him?”

“No.”

The answer came too quickly to be comforting.

“Who did?”

“Security officers assigned to the array.”

“And you covered it up.”

“Yes.”

The word seemed to change the dimensions of the office. The polished walls, the quiet vents, the glowing city below—everything became part of the same sealed room.

“Why?” Tomas asked.

Rusk closed the file. “Because after Darian died, the Council needed someone who understood the danger and would not mistake disclosure for rescue. I was given access to the inner circle. I was told that if I refused, the next failure would be handled without witnesses at all.”

“You joined them.”

“I believed I could limit the harm.”

“You became their voice.”

“I kept the channels open. I prevented wars between the upper districts. I stopped three attempted seizures of the buoyancy controls.”

“And you told everyone the mainland was dead.”

Rusk looked at his son with a grief that arrived too late to be useful. “I told them what would keep Lumen from tearing itself apart.”

“No,” Tomas said. “You told them what kept you from having to choose.”

An alert flashed on the office console. Unauthorized access detected in the lower Ministry. Tomas imagined Jori and the others holding their nine-minute window together with stolen permissions and shaking hands.

“Eli,” he said. “Now.”

Rusk stared at him for a long moment, then entered a command. A restricted file appeared: CENTRAL TOWER, ATMOSPHERIC EVALUATION, SUBJECT E-12. TRANSFER 04:10. ACCESS VIA HOSPITAL SERVICE SPINE. SECURITY ESCORT: SIX.

Tomas copied it to the slate.

“Channel codes,” he said.

His father’s fingers hovered above the console.

“If I give you those, you will broadcast.”

“Yes.”

“You will bring the city down.”

“We are trying to keep it from falling.”

Rusk entered a second sequence. “Emergency channels are not enough. The Council has layered overrides. Use code R-17, then request civilian continuity. Do not trust a single confirmation. Require two stations.”

Tomas recognized the protocol. It was older than the Ministry’s current system, designed for disasters before disaster became policy.

“Why help me?”

Rusk looked again toward the window. “Because Darian was right about the emissions.”

Tomas waited.

“And because I have spent fourteen years calling a murder an accident.”

The office door chimed. Security clearance revoked.

Rusk pushed the black file across the desk. “Take it.”

Tomas did not move. “You should come with me.”

“I cannot.”

“You can.”

“I am not brave enough to be innocent, and I am not innocent enough to be brave.”

The lock began to cycle.

Tomas snatched the file. His hand shook so badly that the pages rattled.

“Did Mara know?” Rusk asked.

“No.”

“Tell her.”

“Tell her yourself.”

The minister’s face collapsed for an instant, not into tears but into something smaller and more terrible: the knowledge that he had forfeited the right to be believed.

Tomas turned the emergency latch. Before leaving, he looked back.

His father was standing beneath the Ministry seal, surrounded by the machinery of a lie he had once called protection.

Then Tomas ran.

Mara was waiting at the junction with Imani and Nia when he returned. She had expected urgency, perhaps triumph. Instead Tomas came down the stairwell pale, carrying the black file against his ribs.

“Eli?” she asked.

“Central tower. Atmospheric evaluation. Transfer at 04:10. Six guards. Service spine access.” He handed her the slate. “I have the channel codes.”

Relief broke across her face, then stopped when she saw the file.

“What is that?”

Tomas looked at her. The corridor hummed around them. Somewhere above, the city announced the coming celebration.

“It is about your father.”

Mara did not take the file. “What about him?”

“He did not die in an accident.”

The words entered her slowly, like cold water through a cracked door.

Tomas opened the file and showed her the report. He told her about Array T-17, the emissions, the sabotage attempt, the security officers, and the Council’s manufactured death. He told her that Minister Rusk had known. He told her that the murder had been used to draw his father into the inner circle, where fear could be made into policy and policy could be made to sound like mercy.

Mara listened without interrupting.

When he finished, she took the report. Her eyes moved over the correction in red ink.

“Who killed him?”

“Security officers. My father said he did not order it.”

“Did he stop it?”

“No.”

She folded the page once. Then again.

For years, her father had been a closed door in the family: a careful silence, a reported accident, a missing explanation. She had mourned the shape of him without knowing what shape it was. Now grief returned with an edge. He had not simply died. He had chosen something. He had seen the lines beneath the official map and tried to break them.

Pride rose first, hot and dangerous.

Then anger came for it.

“Why did no one tell me?” she asked.

“Because the Council buried it.”

“My mother knew?”

“I do not know.”

Mara looked toward the hospital arrow. The map in her hand trembled.

Her father had tried to expose the truth and been killed for it. She had spent years believing the city’s boundaries were necessary. She had drawn routes for the people who erased him. The knowledge did not make her feel chosen. It made her feel late.

Tomas stepped closer. “Mara—”

“Do not apologize for him.”

“I was not.”

“Do not ask me to understand.”

“I am not.”

She looked at him then, and saw the same wound in a different uniform: a son carrying the confession of a father who had mistaken obedience for protection.

“I hate him,” Tomas said quietly. “I think I still love him. I do not know what to do with both.”

Mara pressed the report against her chest. “Neither do I.”

Imani checked the corridor clock. “We have less than two hours.”

Nia tightened a coupling on her tool harness. “Then grief can walk.”

Mara almost laughed. Instead she placed the file inside her map case, beside the routes meant to save Eli and the people who would be caught in the coming descent.

“First the hospital,” she said. “Then the broadcast.”

Tomas nodded.

“And when this is over,” Mara continued, “we open every archive. Every order. Every name.”

Imani’s expression was wary. “That is a promise you can keep only if people help you keep it.”

Mara looked at the arrows on the wall. Hospital. Ministry. No return.

“My father tried to break one hidden line,” she said. “We are going to make the whole map visible.”

They turned toward the hospital service route. Behind them, deep in the Broadcast Ministry, a sealed office continued to glow above the lower rings. Ahead, the central tower waited with its locked doors, its guarded patient, and the machinery of a city preparing to call its own fear salvation.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old former Lumen apprentice cartographer, currently in the hospital service route beneath Ring Seven with Tomas, Imani, and Nia after splitting briefly from Tomas at the Broadcast Ministry. She carries her waterproof route map, notebook, drafting tools, collaborative relay maps, recorder, grease pencil, forged maintenance identification, illegal public-use survival map, and now the black file documenting her father Darian Venn’s murder. She knows Eli is in central tower atmospheric evaluation with transfer scheduled for 04:10, guarded by six officers, and has emergency channel protocol R-17 with two-station verification. set.name: Sela Venn

set.name: Tomas Rusk

set.name: Imani Okafor
set.description: Former Lumen atmospheric engineer, currently in the hospital service route beneath Ring Seven with Mara, Tomas, and Nia. chapters.name: The Hospital of Useful Lives
chapters.content:
The hospital service line narrowed as it climbed toward the central tower. Pipes crowded the ceiling, wrapped in sweating insulation. Every few steps, a valve shuddered and released a breath of warm metal-scented air. Mara followed the blue maintenance stripe on the wall, one hand pressed to her map case and the other against her bruised shoulder.

At the final junction, Tomas stopped.

The hospital route continued through a pressure door. A second passage rose toward the Ministry relay, where the emergency channels waited behind three layers of authorization.

“I go up,” he said.

Mara’s first response was no. It arrived so quickly that she had to swallow it before speaking. “You just came back.”

“And now I have to keep the codes alive.” He held up the forged slate. “R-17 will reject a command unless the Ministry confirms civilian continuity. If the channel drops, the hospital’s internal systems will lock down.”

Imani checked the pressure gauge beside the door. “How long can you maintain the loop?”

“Jori’s people have nine minutes of borrowed access. I can extend it if I reach the relay desk.”

Nia adjusted the straps of her tool harness. “And if security recognizes you?”

“They already recognize me.”

“That was not reassurance.”

“No.” Tomas looked at Mara. He had not mentioned the black file again, but she could feel its presence inside her case, a weight beside the maps. “Get Eli out. Get as many of the others out as you can. I will bring the channels.”

Mara wanted to ask whether his father had given him the codes willingly, whether the minister was still alive, whether Tomas had left him surrounded by the machinery of his own lies. Instead she said, “Two-station confirmation.”

“Never trust one voice.”

“Not even yours.”

A tired smile touched his mouth. “Especially not mine.”

He pressed his forehead briefly to hers. Then he turned toward the rising passage.

“Come back,” Mara said.

“I’ll try.”

“That is not enough.”

“It is what I have.”

He disappeared into the service dark.

The pressure door opened with a reluctant clang. Cold air rolled over them, sharp with disinfectant. Beyond it lay the research hospital: a sequence of white corridors suspended inside the tower, all glass partitions and sealed observation rooms. The public hospitals in the lower rings were crowded, patched, and loud. This place was almost silent. Its cleanliness seemed less like care than concealment.

Nia found the first camera and lifted a small mirror from her harness. “Three lenses. One blind angle.”

“Can you hold it?” Imani asked.

“Long enough.”

Mara crossed first, keeping her face lowered beneath the maintenance hood. The corridor lights brightened as she passed. On the other side, she waited while Imani slipped through, then Nia. Nia pulled the mirror away. The camera resumed its slow sweep.

A wall display showed the hospital’s guiding principle in blue letters:

EVERY LIFE CONTRIBUTES TO CONTINUITY.

Below it, smaller text listed the current research divisions.

Atmospheric adaptation.
Respiratory endurance.
Pressure response.
Civic viability assessment.

Mara stopped.

“Civic viability,” she said.

Imani’s face hardened. “Keep moving.”

They reached the records vestibule using an access token Tomas had copied from the transfer data. A panel asked for the patient classification. Mara entered E-12.

The screen displayed Eli’s name, age, blood type, and a yellow triangle.

SUBJECT: VENN, ELIAS.
STATUS: CONTINUOUS SUPPORT.
TRIAL GROUP: A-9.
PROJECTED DATA VALUE: HIGH.

Mara’s fingers tightened around the slate.

“Data value,” Nia whispered. “They put that on children?”

“On everyone,” Imani said. “They just use different words for people they intend to lose.”

A second file opened automatically. Mara expected dosage charts. Instead she saw a list of names, hundreds of them, each divided into columns. Citizenship tier. Occupational function. Dependents. Trial suitability. Projected recovery. Acceptable loss.

At the bottom, a note had been signed by the Council Medical Directorate:

LOW-VALUE POPULATIONS MAY BE USED FOR ACCELERATED EXPOSURE PROTOCOLS WHERE CONSENT IS UNAVAILABLE OR ADMINISTRATIVELY IMPRACTICAL.

The room seemed to tilt.

“Copy it,” Imani said.

Mara photographed the page with her recorder, then connected the drafting slate to the terminal. Files poured across the screen: families denied Lumenex while the same compound was tested in higher concentrations on selected patients; respiratory treatments shelved because their distribution would “alter labor allocation”; children transferred from lower rings under emergency classifications; death records revised after failed trials.

A red line ran down the side of several files.

EXPENDABLE TEST POPULATION.

Mara read the phrase until the letters lost their meaning. Then she saw Eli’s name among the subjects and understood that the hospital had not mistaken him for a patient. It had identified him correctly as someone the city believed no one important would defend.

Imani touched the screen. “Here.”

She opened a treatment protocol from an unrecognized source. The header was written in mainland notation, with dosage values expressed by body mass rather than citizenship tier.

“Compound?” Mara asked.

“Adaptive bronchodilator with a particulate-binding carrier.” Imani scanned the instructions. “This is the Tilbury treatment. Or a version of it.”

“Can it save him?”

“It can stabilize him. It cannot reverse the damage already done.”

“Then take it.”

Imani scrolled farther. Her expression changed. “They have the medicine.”

A storage location appeared: RESEARCH PHARMACY, CABINET FOUR, SEALED ACCESS.

“Why have they not given it to him?” Nia asked.

“Because the trial is measuring whether his lungs adapt without it,” Imani said. “If they administer a treatment that works, they lose the result.”

Mara felt something inside her become very quiet.

“Where is he?”

The terminal marked his room in the atmospheric evaluation ward, two levels above. Transfer countdown: one hour, forty-three minutes.

They left the vestibule through a linen passage. Imani moved with the confidence of someone who understood hospital machinery, if not its corridors. Nia carried a portable oxygen cylinder under her coat and had modified its coupling to fit two kinds of masks. Mara carried the stolen patient list in her recorder and kept Eli’s route bright in her mind.

At the pharmacy door, a technician looked up.

“Maintenance is restricted.”

“Filter pressure fault,” Nia said, before Mara could answer. “Cabinet four is overloading the seal.”

The technician glanced at her tool harness. “You’re not pharmacy maintenance.”

“I’m not asking you to diagnose it.”

Imani leaned toward the panel. “If the seal ruptures, you lose the respiratory compounds.”

That did it. The technician swore and opened the door.

Inside, the air smelled of alcohol and cold plastic. Cabinet four required two keys. Nia produced a coupling shaped like a key and fitted it into the lower port while Imani used Tomas’s authorization on the upper reader. The lock resisted, flashed amber, then opened.

Three ampoules rested inside a foam cradle. Their labels were in mainland script. Beside them sat a printed administration card, folded and stained at one corner.

Imani took the ampoules. “One for Eli. Two for anyone whose lungs fail during the transfer.”

“Can we make more?”

“Not here. The carrier needs a low-pressure mixer and sterile nebulizer.”

“Does the ward have those?”

“It has both. It has decided who may use them.”

The alarm began before the pharmacy door had fully closed.

Not a siren. A soft chime, repeated at measured intervals.

Nia froze. “That is not a fire alert.”

“No,” Imani said. “It is a patient-integrity breach.”

Mara’s recorder vibrated. A message from Tomas appeared on its dark screen.

CHANNEL LOOP ACTIVE. SECURITY SEARCHING LOWER HOSPITAL. TWO-STATION CONFIRMATION PENDING.

“They know,” Mara said.

“Then we stop being quiet,” Imani replied.

They ran.

The atmospheric ward occupied a circular level above the pharmacy. Its rooms were arranged around a central observation well, each one sealed behind transparent walls. Patients lay beneath angled lamps with tubes at their noses and wrists. Some were children. Some were old enough to have grandchildren. All had numbers displayed beside their beds.

E-12 was at the far end.

Eli looked smaller than Mara remembered. His hair was damp against his forehead, and a clear mask covered his mouth and nose. A line ran from his arm to a machine pulsing with pale green light. His eyes opened when Mara entered.

For one terrible second, he did not recognize her.

Then he lifted his hand.

“Mara?”

She pressed her palm to the glass. “I’m here.”

His voice came through the room speaker as a thread of static. “You took long enough.”

Nia laughed once, a broken sound. Imani was already at the door controls.

“The ward is locked to central control,” she said. “I can override the patient seal, but his support will drop during the transfer.”

“How long?” Mara asked.

“Thirty seconds, perhaps less.”

“Do it.”

Imani looked at her. “We need the nebulizer first.”

Nia ran to the equipment station and began disconnecting a portable unit. “This one has a pressure regulator.”

“Second reading,” Imani said.

Nia checked the gauge, then checked it again with a hand instrument. “Regulator is stable. Oxygen flow is low.”

“Raise it by one mark.”

“On your count.”

Imani entered the override. The door opened. Mara reached Eli as the machines shifted from green to amber.

“Don’t pull the line,” she told him.

“I know.”

“You always say that.”

“You always tell me things I know.”

His fingers closed around hers. They were cold.

Imani fitted the mainland ampoule into the nebulizer. “Eli, this may make you cough.”

“Will it hurt?”

“Yes,” Imani said. “But it should help you breathe.”

Mara looked at her sharply.

“What?” Imani said. “He deserves the truth.”

Eli nodded as if that settled it. Nia attached the mask while Imani counted the flow. Eli coughed immediately, his whole body tightening. Mara held his shoulders. The cough became a tearing rattle, then eased. The monitor dipped, recovered, dipped again.

“Come on,” Mara whispered.

The line on the screen steadied by degrees.

Eli’s next breath came deeper.

Not easy. Not healed. But deeper.

“Treatment is working,” Imani said. “We move now.”

Across the ward, a patient in the nearest room struck the glass with a trembling hand. “Take me.”

Another voice called, “Please.”

Mara stared at the rows of beds. The records had named them expendable. The patients had names of their own, but the hospital had hidden them behind numbers.

“How many can we carry?” she asked.

“Four with portable support,” Nia said. “Maybe five if we use the transport frame.”

Imani looked toward the corridor. “Security will be here in under two minutes.”

The patient nearest them was a girl perhaps fifteen years old, her lips blue around an oxygen mask. “My name is Lio,” she said. “I am not a number.”

Mara went to her door.

“Imani?”

A pause. Then: “Four.”

Nia released the first seal. Mara and Imani moved quickly, transferring Lio, an older man with pressure injuries, and two younger children onto portable rigs. The machines complained as they were unplugged. Every alarm sounded like an accusation.

In the observation well, the patient list remained open on the central terminal. Mara reached through the access panel and pulled the data core free.

“Evidence,” she said.

“People first,” Imani answered.

“Both.”

Boots struck the corridor outside.

Nia shoved the transport frame toward the service exit. “Route?”

Mara unfolded her waterproof map with one hand while steadying Eli’s cylinder with the other. “North stairwell is sealed. Laundry lift goes down to Ring Seven, but the lower hospital is already under search.”

“Then up,” Imani said.

“Central tower.”

“Toward Tomas?”

“Toward the broadcast relay.”

They pushed into the corridor just as two security officers appeared at the far end. Behind them came a medical administrator in a white coat.

“Return the subjects,” the administrator ordered. “You are compromising active trials.”

Mara stopped. Eli’s hand found the back of her coat.

“These are patients,” she said.

“They are classified research populations.”

“People,” Lio rasped from the transport frame.

The administrator’s face tightened. “You do not understand the consequences of unauthorized release.”

Mara lifted the recorder. “I understand the records. I understand that you had the treatment and withheld it. I understand that you called children expendable.”

One officer raised a shock baton.

The corridor lights flickered. Tomas’s voice burst from the ceiling speakers, distorted but unmistakable.

“Emergency protocol R-17 active. Civilian continuity confirmed by Station North and Station Seven. All medical personnel are ordered to preserve life. Repeat: preserve life.”

The officer hesitated.

From another speaker, a woman’s voice repeated the order. Then a third. The hospital’s own intercom began to echo with confirmations from stations Mara could not see.

“Two stations,” Imani said softly.

“More than two,” Nia replied.

The administrator lunged for the nearest control panel. Mara threw the drafting slate. It struck his wrist, and the command failed. Imani seized the transport frame and pushed.

“Move!”

They ran toward the central lift while alarms multiplied behind them. Doors opened along the ward. Nurses emerged, some carrying masks, some simply standing in the corridors as if waking from a long sleep. One nurse took Lio’s hand. Another blocked the security officers with a medication cart.

Mara looked back only once.

The hospital’s blue slogan still glowed above them: EVERY LIFE CONTRIBUTES TO CONTINUITY.

For the first time, it sounded less like a principle than a demand the city might be forced to honor.

The central lift doors opened. Inside, a maintenance crew waited with tools raised. Mara recognized none of them, but one worker wore a Ring Eight filter patch on her sleeve.

“Sela sent word,” the woman said. “The lower rings are opening doors.”

Mara pushed Eli inside. Imani and Nia followed with the other patients.

“Where does this go?” Nia asked.

“Central tower relay,” Mara said.

The lift began to rise.

Eli’s breathing remained shallow, but the monitor held steady. Mara crouched beside him, clutching the treatment card and the stolen data core. Around her, strangers made room for patients the Council had calculated as losses.

Above them waited the emergency studio, the Crown Seal controls, and a city that still did not know what had been done in its name.

Tomas’s voice came through the lift speaker, quieter now. “Mara, we have the channel for another window. Get to the tower.”

She looked at Eli. His eyes were closed, but his fingers still held hers.

“We’re coming,” she said.

The lift climbed into the machinery of the city, carrying the useful lives that Lumen had tried to spend.
