chapters.name: The Emergency Channels
chapters.content:
The Broadcast Ministry had been built to make a lie feel like weather.

Its walls were curved, soundless, and white, designed to carry a minister’s voice without echo. Every studio opened onto a control gallery where operators could watch the city’s response in colored bars: calm, concern, disorder, threat. Tomas had spent years believing those colors described reality. Now the red bands pulsed across every screen while the building trembled beneath the falling city.

“Open the emergency channel,” he said.

The operator at the primary console did not look at him. “Authorization denied.”

“You have R-17.”

“R-17 requires ministerial release.”

Tomas placed his forged access slate on the console. The screen rejected it, accepted it, then displayed his father’s name in a red box.

MINISTERIAL AUTHORITY REQUIRED.

Behind him, Jori Pell shut the studio door. Two former Ministry technicians stood at the secondary stations, listening to voices break across the internal mesh.

“Ring Six is losing pressure,” one said. “The lower clinics are asking whether the western shelters are open.”

“Platform mechanics report Council drones firing on the access walks,” said another. “They’re trying to clear the upper gardens.”

Tomas turned back to the operator. “Open the channel.”

“I cannot.”

“You can, or you can watch people die while the system waits for a name.”

The operator’s hands remained folded. “My authorization is limited.”

A door at the rear of the gallery opened. Minister Rusk entered with four security officers.

His father wore the dark formal coat of the Council, though the collar had come loose and one sleeve was wet with condensation. He looked older than he had an hour before. Older than he had looked when he explained that Darian Venn had been killed for trying to tell the truth. Yet his expression was composed, the same expression that had appeared on every broadcast during every shortage, flood, and unexplained death.

Order, Tomas thought. The face of order.

“Leave us,” Rusk said.

“No,” Tomas answered.

The officers raised their weapons a fraction.

Rusk studied his son. “You have made yourself difficult to protect.”

“I am not asking you to protect me.”

“You are asking me to open channels that will turn panic into a stampede.”

“I am asking for the mainland relay coordinates.”

“The mainland is not a rescue service.”

“It has hospitals. Engineers. Working settlements. People who have been answering our relays.”

“People who will use this moment to enter Lumen.”

“People we poisoned.”

The words struck the gallery and seemed to stay there. On the nearest screen, the city map lurched sideways. A whole district of light vanished, then returned in scattered points.

Rusk’s gaze moved to the display. “The Crown Seal is stabilizing the city.”

“It is making the city dependent on its own enclosure.”

“Because the alternatives were worse.”

“You knew it was already active.”

“I knew enough to understand that disclosure would destroy public cooperation.”

“No. You knew enough to keep people obedient.”

One of the officers stepped forward. “Minister, the emergency studio must be secured.”

Rusk lifted a hand. “My son is still under the illusion that truth is an instrument. He thinks if we place the right facts before frightened people, they will make the right decisions.”

Tomas felt the old anger rise, clean and familiar. “And you think obedience makes decisions right.”

“I think a city cannot survive if every citizen is invited to question every instruction.”

“Then why are the upper families breaking through their own gates?”

Rusk’s face tightened.

The Ministry’s external feed had begun showing the eastern districts. Elite residents in bright coats crowded an access bridge, carrying children, medical cases, and cases of food. They had attempted to leave the sealed residential rings and reach the lower transit hubs. Security barriers blocked them. A woman in a silver coat pressed both hands against a shield and shouted at the officers. Behind her, a boy coughed into his father’s sleeve.

The officers raised their rifles.

“Tell them to stand down,” Tomas said.

Rusk did not move. “The barrier is protecting the transit corridor.”

“They are civilians.”

“They are obstructing evacuation.”

“They are trying to evacuate.”

A burst of white light crossed the feed. The crowd recoiled. For one impossible second Tomas saw the woman in silver standing alone, her hands still lifted. Then the image fractured into static.

The operator whispered, “They fired.”

No one in the gallery breathed.

Rusk’s voice remained low. “The officers were instructed to preserve the corridor.”

“By shooting people?”

“By preventing a breach.”

Another feed opened automatically. Lower-ring workers had overturned a security vehicle near Ring Seven. Officers were firing into the smoke. Someone dragged an injured guard behind a vending kiosk. Someone else was waving a white cloth.

Tomas looked at his father. “There is no order here.”

“There is a city under emergency conditions.”

“There is a regime killing anyone it cannot control.”

Rusk’s eyes hardened. “Mind your language.”

“Why? Are you going to arrest me again?”

“You are alive because I delayed the order.”

“You are alive because Mara and the mainland rescued the patients you classified as expendable.”

For the first time, Rusk looked away.

Tomas moved to the console. “Release the channels.”

“Stand down,” said one of the officers.

Jori stepped between them. “If you shoot him, the studio loses its only working authorization pattern.”

The officer glanced at Rusk.

That hesitation told Tomas more than any confession. The Ministry was no longer obeying one voice. It was calculating which future might preserve it.

Rusk came to the console. “If I release the coordinates, every station will receive instructions from outside the city. Some will open their gates. Some will cut power. Some will attack the Council.”

“Some will save people.”

“Some will save themselves first.”

“Yes,” Tomas said. “That is what people do when their government has abandoned them.”

His father’s hand hovered above the authorization panel. The screen displayed the mainland relay list: Tilbury, northern bank, Gravesend, former university, unnamed coastal stations whose signals had only recently returned. Behind each coordinate was a warning: unverified, disputed, local confirmation required.

Mara’s system. No single command. Trust more than one person.

“Order requires obedience,” Rusk said.

Tomas remembered the central chamber, the three keys, the witness chain. He remembered Mara leaving the console because a map was not a throne. “Survival requires information.”

“Information without control is a weapon.”

“Then stop hiding it.”

Rusk stared at the relay list. His fingers trembled once. He closed them into a fist.

The external feed showed the eastern bridge again. The silver-coated woman was gone. Security officers were forcing families back toward the sealed district. Among them were two Council members Tomas recognized from ceremonial broadcasts. Their insignia did not protect them. The officers shoved one of them to the ground.

Rusk watched.

“They will not stop,” Tomas said. “Not when they reach the lower rings. Not when they reach the hospitals. Not when they reach this room.”

“They are following emergency directives.”

“They are following people who will sacrifice anyone necessary.”

Rusk’s mouth opened, but no defense came.

A shot cracked somewhere beyond the gallery doors. The technicians flinched. The building lights dimmed. Across the city map, red bands spread through the upper districts.

Rusk placed his palm on the authorization panel.

The system asked for voice confirmation.

“Minister Elias Rusk,” he said. “Release emergency protocol R-17. Open all continuity channels. Transmit mainland relay coordinates and local verification rules.”

The panel flashed amber.

Tomas stared at him. “And the historical archive.”

Rusk’s hand remained against the glass.

“Transmit the founders’ records,” Tomas said. “The evacuation lists. The emissions reports. Everything.”

“That will destroy the Ministry.”

“It should.”

Rusk looked at his son then—not as an official, not as a minister, but as the man who had once taught Tomas to identify constellations through the city’s false dawn. “Your mother believed secrecy was temporary.”

Tomas thought of the files, the withheld treatments, the empty hospital beds. “You made it permanent.”

His father swallowed. “I believed I was preserving a future.”

“You preserved a hierarchy.”

“I preserved you.”

“No,” Tomas said. “You preserved a city where someone else’s child could be spent to keep me safe.”

Rusk’s face collapsed—not into repentance, exactly, but recognition. The distinction mattered less than the act that followed.

He spoke into the panel. “Release all restricted historical records.”

The Ministry opened.

For three seconds nothing happened. Then the emergency mesh erupted. Coordinates streamed across every surviving channel. Local thresholds followed. So did the Council’s sealed orders, the manufactured mainland maps, the emissions memoranda, the hospital classifications, and the names of officers who had altered the records.

Across Lumen, screens changed from the Council seal to a field of ordinary text.

A technician began to cry without noticing.

Rusk leaned toward the microphone. “Citizens of Lumen,” he said. “The history taught by this Ministry was manufactured. The mainland was not dead. We concealed inhabited settlements, redirected atmospheric damage toward them, and withheld treatment while assigning value to lives. The Crown Seal was built to make our isolation permanent. I authorized broadcasts that described survivors as threats. I signed orders that concealed evacuation plans. I believed order could excuse the means by which it was maintained.”

His voice faltered.

Tomas reached for the transmit control. “Keep going.”

Rusk nodded once. “The mainland relay coordinates are now public. No station is to accept a command without local confirmation and a second witness. Do not destroy the relays. Do not attack civilians. If you can open a clinic, shelter, garden, or oxygen store, open it. If an officer orders you to close one, verify the order through two independent stations.”

The gallery doors buckled.

One officer turned toward them. “Minister, terminate transmission.”

Rusk did not.

The door burst inward. Security entered firing.

The first shot struck the console. The second struck Rusk below the ribs. He folded against the microphone, dragging the cable loose. A third shot hit his shoulder and spun him onto the floor.

“Tomas!” Jori shouted.

Tomas dropped behind the secondary station as glass and sparks scattered across the gallery. The technicians crouched beneath the consoles. One of the officers advanced, weapon aimed at the fallen minister.

Rusk’s hand found the microphone.

“Continue,” he whispered.

The open channel carried it everywhere.

Tomas crawled to the transmit board. Blood spread beneath his father’s coat, dark against the white floor. Rusk looked at him, and for a moment Tomas was again a child waiting for the next instruction.

“Do not make me the reason you stop,” Rusk said.

Then the officer fired again.

The channel remained open.

Tomas seized the control key. “All stations, this is emergency continuity. Ministerial authorization has been released. Repeat: ministerial authorization has been released. The coordinates are valid only with local verification. Record every failure. Report every obstruction. Do not wait for central rescue.”

A voice from Tilbury answered first. “Tilbury confirms receipt.”

“Northern bank confirms.”

“Ring Eight confirms. Clinics remain open.” Sela’s voice, strained but steady.

From somewhere in the central tower came Imani. “Central confirms the authorization pattern. Tomas, are you able to continue?”

He looked at his father’s body. The gallery smelled of hot circuitry and blood. His hands shook so violently he had to brace one against the console.

“I am able,” he said.

It was not true in the way old Ministry statements had been true. He was not unafraid. He was not whole. He did not know whether the city would survive the next hour or whether his father’s confession would prevent violence or feed it.

But the channel did not require certainty. It required a witness.

“Publish the shooting,” Tomas told Jori. “Publish the names of the officers. Do not edit the death.”

Jori stared at him. “Your father—”

“His death is part of the record.”

The officers fled as distant alarms converged. No one pursued them. The Ministry technicians began routing the broadcast through the newly opened relays, handing control from station to station.

On the central map, green signals appeared beneath the red.

Mara’s voice entered the mesh from the west platform. “Tomas, we received the coordinates. The outer teams are moving. What happened?”

Tomas closed his eyes once. “My father released the channels. Security shot him.”

Silence answered.

Then Mara said, “Are you still at the Ministry?”

“Yes.”

“Can you keep the emergency mesh running?”

He looked at the blood on the floor, at the open records, at the thousands of people now hearing the truth without a minister to contain it.

“Yes,” he said again. “But not alone.”

Across the city, stations repeated the instruction. Two confirmations. Local authority. Report uncertainty. Keep doors open.

The Broadcast Ministry had been built to make a lie feel like weather.

Now, for the first time, it carried the storm honestly.

chapters.name: The Outer Platforms
chapters.content:
The first outer platform had no walls.

There was only a rib of metal extending from Lumen’s lower hull into the storm, its grated floor shining with rain and condensate. Beyond the rail, the city fell away in terraces of light. Below that, cloud boiled over the dark Atlantic, torn open now and then to show fragments of drowned coastline.

Nia clipped her safety line to the first cable and tested it with both hands. The cable groaned.

“Not that one,” she said.

A young man behind her looked at the sagging line. His jacket bore the silver stripe of Upper Civic Engineering. The woman beside him wore the gray patch of Ring Eight filtration labor. Neither had spoken since the maintenance hatch opened.

Nia pointed to the cable. “If it breaks, it takes the three of us with it. We use the lower line and keep one hand on the rail.”

“The lower line is marked condemned,” the young man said.

“By whom?”

He glanced toward the security camera mounted above the hatch. “The Council systems.”

“Then the Council systems can come out here and explain why.”

The woman in gray laughed once, unexpectedly. It was a small sound, almost lost in the wind.

Nia looked back at the team. There were nine of them: mechanics, filtration workers, a retired lift operator, two students from an engineering school, and a boy who had lied about being sixteen until the woman in gray threatened to send him back inside. They had come from districts that had spent their lives being told not to trust one another. Now all of them wore borrowed harnesses and carried tools in the same battered canvas bags.

“Mara,” Nia called. “Route.”

Mara crouched beside the open hatch, one knee pressed into the wet decking. Her waterproof map was spread beneath a transparent sheet, weighted at the corners by bolts. The printed lines had been made years ago in the Office of Cartography, when routes had been symbols and workers had been numbers. Mara had drawn the official service lanes in clean blue ink. Later, in pencil and grease, she had added what the official map omitted: handholds, locked doors, narrow crawlways, pipes that grew hot before a pressure surge, and the names of people who knew which shortcuts were safe.

She traced a line with her finger.

“Platform Six is open to Junction H,” she said. “But the western strut is flexing. We don’t cross it. We go below the maintenance spine, climb at the old inspection ladder, and come up behind the engine housing.”

“The old ladder is gone,” said the young man.

Mara looked up. “How do you know?”

“I serviced this platform last winter.”

“Then mark it gone.”

He hesitated.

Mara held out the grease pencil. “Not on my map. On everyone’s.”

He took it. On the clear sheet, he drew a black cross over the ladder.

“What’s your name?” Nia asked.

“Jalen.”

“Jalen, you lead the lower spine. You’ve seen it recently. If it’s changed since winter, stop and report it. Don’t make the map true by dying for it.”

His expression shifted, as if nobody had ever offered him an order that included permission to refuse.

“All right,” he said.

The hatch opened wider. Wind punched through the maintenance bay and lifted loose papers from the wall. Somewhere inside the city, alarms were sounding in three different rhythms. One announced pressure loss. One announced unauthorized movement. The third had begun as a warning about the Crown Seal and ended in a flat mechanical repetition: DESCENT IRREGULAR. DESCENT IRREGULAR.

Tomas’s voice came through their headsets, broken by static.

“West teams, confirm personnel before crossing. We have two-station confirmation from Tilbury and Gravesend. Northern bank relay is charging. Do not report success unless local readings and an independent station agree.”

Nia pressed her transmitter. “Outer west team, nine personnel, one apprentice too young, one retired lift operator too old, and seven people with more sense than the Ministry. Proceeding to Junction H.”

“Received,” Tomas said. His voice was hoarse. “For the record, the apprentice is sixteen.”

“I’m seventeen,” the boy protested.

“You told me sixteen,” Nia said.

“I told you what would make you let me come.”

“Then you’re a liar and a mechanic. Stay behind me.”

They stepped onto the platform.

The metal shook beneath their boots. Not from the wind alone. Lumen was descending, though the change was so gradual that the body registered it only as wrongness: the horizon rising, the rails pulling at their harnesses, the city’s distant towers leaning by a degree too many.

Mara watched the altimeter clipped to her wrist. “Point three meters per minute,” she said.

“Current?”

“Point five.”

No one spoke for several seconds.

Below them, through a break in the cloud, the mainland appeared. Tilbury’s elevated structures glimmered along the old transport hub, and farther west small lights moved along roads that had once been rivers. The low settlements were evacuating. Tomas relayed their reports as they came: boats leaving the reed islands, carts climbing toward the old rail embankments, clinic teams carrying oxygen cylinders uphill. The voices were calm because people had work to do. Their calm frightened Mara more than shouting would have.

At the end of Platform Six, the condemned cable dipped toward a junction box half hidden in a cage of struts. A cloud of yellowish vapor curled from the box and vanished in the wind.

“Condensate,” said the filtration worker. “Toxic?”

“Probably,” said Jalen.

“Probably is not a reading,” Nia said.

The retired lift operator, whose name was Besh, produced a small hand meter from his coat. He held it into the vapor. The device clicked rapidly.

“Ammonia compounds and particulate metals,” he said. “Mask up. Short exposure only.”

Nia looked at the box. “The cable coupling is inside.”

“Then we make short exposure shorter.”

They divided without argument. Jalen and the two students prepared the replacement coupling. The woman in gray, whose name was Reva, checked everyone’s seals. Nia crawled beneath the strut with a wrench between her teeth and a second pressure gauge clipped to her harness. Mara stayed at the hatch side, reading the map and the changing figures from the central chamber.

A siren shrieked.

The camera above the platform turned toward them. Its lens opened like a pupil.

“Unauthorized maintenance personnel,” announced a voice. “Remain in place for civic verification.”

“Civic verification can wait,” Nia muttered.

The camera emitted a sharp pulse. A panel along the railing slid open, revealing a compact defense drone. Its targeting light swept across the workers.

Jalen froze.

Mara saw the old route before she saw the drone’s weapon. On the map, beneath the platform, the maintenance spine curved around the engine housing. A manual isolation hatch was marked with the cartographer’s symbol for obsolete access. She had drawn it herself years ago, then removed it from the public version because the corridor crossed a restricted boundary.

“Jalen,” she called. “Three meters left. There’s an isolation wheel below the rail.”

“I don’t see it.”

“Your boot, by the drain.”

He felt with his foot, found the wheel, and turned it. A shield of folded metal sprang up from the platform edge. The drone fired. The impact struck the shield and threw sparks over the deck.

“Move!” Nia shouted.

The team dragged the coupling and tools behind the shield. The drone fired again. The railing buckled, but the old metal held.

“Mara,” Tomas said in her headset, “we have an automated defense activation at Junction H. Can you confirm whether the station is still under Council command?”

“It is shooting at workers.”

“That is not a system classification.”

“It is now.”

She heard him breathe, then heard other voices behind him: reports from Ring Four, a flooded access shaft, a mainland station that had lost its second confirmation. The mesh was not a smooth command line. It was a room full of people speaking through walls while the walls moved.

“Nia,” Mara said, “the defense circuit is fed through the engine housing. If you isolate the west bus, the drone should lose power, but Junction H will lose its local control.”

“How long can the junction run without it?”

“Unknown.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Thirty seconds before the pressure differential changes. Maybe ninety.”

Nia grinned fiercely. “There’s your number.”

She threw a hand signal. Reva and Jalen braced the shield while Nia and the two students ran low across the deck. One student reached the housing and slammed the isolation lever down. The drone’s light went dark.

At once, the platform dropped half a handspan.

Someone screamed. The cable coupling tore loose, whipping across the deck. Nia caught it around the waist before it could fall through the grating. Mara saw the strain pull Nia’s harness against the rail.

“Let go!” Jalen shouted.

“It’s the relay cable!”

“It’s killing you!”

Nia planted both boots. “Then help me hold it.”

Jalen seized the cable. Reva joined him, then Besh. The young man from Upper Engineering crawled out from behind the shield and wrapped his arms around the housing brace.

“On three,” Nia said. “One. Two. Three.”

Together they hauled the cable back onto the platform.

The cable was heavier than it looked, thick as a person’s arm and hot beneath its insulation. Nia’s gloves smoked. She released it only when Jalen had locked it into the temporary clamp.

“Second reading,” she said.

The upper-district engineer raised his gauge. Reva checked with another.

“Pressure rising,” he said.

“Pressure holding,” Reva said.

Nia looked at Mara.

Mara compared the figures with the central report. “Local readings disagree by twelve percent.”

“Then we don’t redirect the engine.”

The engineer stared at her. “If we wait, the city loses another two meters.”

“If we redirect on a bad reading, the platform tears itself open.”

He looked toward the cloud. “People below don’t have time for your rules.”

“They are not my rules,” Mara said. “They are the reason we still have people to save.”

Tomas’s voice crackled through. “Junction H, report.”

Nia answered. “Cable seated. Defense isolated. Pressure disagreement twelve percent. No engine redirect yet. Request independent station.”

“Tilbury is calculating.”

“Tell Tilbury to calculate faster.”

“Already told them.”

For a moment, the only sounds were wind and the deep, laboring thrum of the buoyancy engines.

Then a new voice entered the channel. It belonged to a mainland engineer at Gravesend, a woman named Priya whom Mara had never met.

“Junction H, I have your return signal,” Priya said. “Your local pressure is dropping, not rising. The upper gauge is reading condensate heat as pressure. Do not redirect until the lower valve is cleared.”

Nia turned to the upper-district engineer. “You heard her.”

He looked embarrassed, then angry at the embarrassment. “I trained on calibrated systems.”

“Today you train on a broken one.”

She pointed to the lower valve. “Jalen, Reva, with me. Besh, keep the brace. Everyone else, clear the walkway and mark the retreat path.”

Mara unfolded the map farther. “The valve is beneath the inspection cage. There’s an access panel here.”

“That panel was welded shut,” Jalen said.

“Then use the emergency crawlway.”

“You said it crossed a restricted boundary.”

“I did.” Mara folded the official map backward, exposing the pencil layer underneath. “The boundary was invented to keep workers from reaching the pressure controls. It is not a wall.”

They opened the crawlway.

The work took eleven minutes. It felt like an hour. Nia and the others crawled through heat, grease, and metallic vapor while Mara relayed dimensions and route changes from the hatch. Twice the platform lurched. Once, the city’s entire outer rim groaned, a sound so broad it seemed to come from the ocean.

On the mainland, the relays answered one by one.

Tilbury confirmed a stable return. Gravesend confirmed the timing offset. A station near the old northern bank reported a damaged antenna but a usable signal. Other communities moved uphill as the weather twisted above them. Tomas read each report aloud, naming the station, the witness, and the uncertainty.

When Nia finally emerged, her face was black with grease and her left sleeve was burned through. She carried a clogged valve filter in one hand.

“Now,” she said.

Mara checked the gauges. The readings matched within three percent.

“Now,” she agreed.

Nia and the upper-district engineer turned the redirect wheels together. For one terrible second, nothing happened. Then the engine’s note changed. The platform lifted, not much, but enough to stop its downward tilt.

A cheer rose from the workers.

Nia raised a hand. “Don’t celebrate. It’s holding, not fixed.”

Tomas came over the mesh. “Central confirms Junction H is taking load. Mainland relays are beginning the corresponding sequence.”

“How many?” Mara asked.

“Seven answering. Four uncertain. Two silent.”

Nia looked along the exposed platforms. Farther east, one buoyancy engine coughed blue flame. Farther west, another went dark.

“Then we go to the next one,” she said.

Mara rolled up her map. “The next route crosses Platform Nine.”

“Is it safe?”

“No.”

“Is it passable?”

Mara studied the descending city, the cloud-veiled mainland, and the people now moving together beneath the same gray sky.

“Not yet,” she said. “But I know where it used to be.”

Nia picked up the brace kit. “Good. We’ll find out what it became.”

Behind them, Junction H held. Ahead, the platform lights flickered toward darkness, and Lumen continued its slow, dangerous descent.

chapters.name: Open Doors
chapters.content:
The first thing Sela did when the lights went out was put the injured in order of breath.

Not rank. Not age. Not the neat colored bands that had once been stitched into every patient’s sleeve. Breath.

“Names,” she said, standing beneath the filtration block’s failing indicator lamps. “I need names and what you can still do.”

Around her, Ring Eight’s emergency room had been made from a laundry exchange, two storage alcoves, and the corridor outside. The old machines had been pushed against the walls. Sheets hung from pipes to divide the space. A child whimpered behind one curtain while someone hammered at a jammed oxygen cabinet behind another. The floor trembled with a long, low vibration, as if the city had caught a cough too deep to clear.

A woman in a torn security jacket was carried in by two protesters. Blood darkened one side of her face.

“She fired on us,” one of the protesters said.

“She’s bleeding,” Sela answered. “That is what I need to know.”

The protester stared at her, then lowered his eyes. “Her name is Dava.”

“Dava,” Sela repeated, and wrote it on a strip of gauze with a grease pencil. “Pressure on the wound. You—find me clean water. You—check whether the manual filter is drawing. Nobody touches the reserve cylinders without a witness.”

“What tier is she?” asked a frightened volunteer.

Sela looked at the woman’s blood spreading across the jacket. “The kind that leaks.”

The volunteer flushed. “I only meant—”

“I know what you meant. We are not doing it.”

She had no authority now. The compulsory labor roster had vanished when the administration servers began cycling between warning screens. Her housing guarantee, her medical designation, her citizenship credits—none of them mattered in the room. What mattered was whether Dava’s airway closed before the pressure stabilized.

Sela knelt beside the injured officer. Around her, people who had spent their lives being told whom to obey began to work without waiting for permission.

In the west outer platforms, Mara heard none of this directly. She heard it through Tomas’s emergency mesh, broken into clipped packets beneath static and the metallic roar of wind.

“Ring Eight open clinic,” Tomas said in her earpiece. “Sela reports treatment by name. Three confirmed rooms, one oxygen reserve. Ring Four reporting similar. Upper Garden Seven refusing access.”

Mara crouched beneath a maintenance brace while rain—or condensed atmospheric residue—struck the platform above her. Her shoulder throbbed where the old wound had opened. Nia was two spans away, bent over a relay junction with her burned sleeve tied above the elbow. Workers from three citizenship tiers crowded the narrow walkway, passing tools hand to hand.

“Why is Garden Seven refusing?” Mara asked.

“Private wardens. They say the gardens are reserved for registered residents.”

“Registered under a system that is failing.”

“I’m aware.” Tomas’s voice rasped. “I can put you on the public channel.”

Mara looked at the pressure gauge in Nia’s hand, then at the route map sealed beneath her palm. The old instinct rose in her: find the authorized person, locate the proper channel, make the correct request. It was a habit built into every corridor of Lumen.

She pressed the transmit stud.

“This is Mara Venn on the open emergency mesh,” she said. “The Crown Seal has begun descent operations. The following instructions are survival instructions, not Council orders. Any person may verify them through two independent stations. If a station cannot confirm, mark the instruction uncertain and do not conceal the uncertainty.”

The channel carried her voice across the city and, through the mainland relays, beyond it.

“Open sealed gardens and public growing rooms. Unlock emergency shelters. Share oxygen reserves according to immediate medical need. Remove citizenship restrictions from clinics, kitchens, water points, and transit corridors. Preserve pumps, filters, relay controls, and food stores. Do not damage infrastructure because it bears a Council mark. Do not obey armed personnel who order the destruction of life-support systems. Report names, locations, and conditions through the witness ledger.”

She paused, listening to the wind.

“Those who can help, help. Those who cannot move, make noise. If you are afraid, say that you are afraid. Fear is information. It is not a command.”

The transmission clicked away.

For several seconds only static answered. Then messages began arriving so quickly Tomas had to repeat them.

“Garden Seven opened by workers cutting the inner lock.”

“Ring Two oxygen room shared.”

“Shelter Twelve unlocked.”

“Upper district residents blocking lift access.”

“Security at the west transit exchange firing into crowd.”

“Mainland refugees on Platform C being attacked.”

Mara closed her eyes. The city had been waiting for an instruction, but not for one instruction. It had been waiting for a hundred thousand decisions, each made by people who had never been permitted to decide anything important.

“Send the route to Platform C,” she said.

“It’s blocked,” Tomas replied. “A security barricade and a food convoy.”

“Then mark the barricade. Is there another route?”

“Checking.”

Nia looked up from the junction. “Don’t send people toward the west lift. The support ribs are twisting. I can hear the bolts walking.”

Mara caught Tomas before he transmitted. “West lift unsafe. Mark it red. Nia’s local reading.”

“Confirmed,” Tomas said. “Red, with reason.”

A new tremor rolled through the platform. Somewhere outside, an engine gave a shriek and settled into a lower, uneven note. The city tilted enough that a loose toolbox slid toward the railing. Three workers lunged for it together.

“Junction H holding,” Nia announced. “Not repaired. Holding.”

Mara repeated the distinction into the mesh. “Junction H is taking load but is not fully repaired. Do not report success where there is only stability. Teams must state what they know and what they do not.”

“People don’t want uncertainty,” one of the workers said. He was an upper-ring technician with a silver collar torn from his uniform. “They want to know whether they’re going to fall.”

“So do I,” Mara said. “That doesn’t make a guess safer.”

At Ring Eight, Sela had begun treating people from the upper districts. They arrived through service corridors with expensive coats over ordinary clothes, some carrying children, some carrying locked cases of food or medicine. One woman refused to let Sela examine her until the other patients were moved away.

“I have a priority medical seal,” she said, thrusting a metal card toward Sela. “My husband is a senior atmospheric assessor.”

Sela took the card, turned it over, and set it on the floor. “Your husband is not here.”

“He is in Garden Three.”

“Then go tell him the garden is open.”

“My daughter is unconscious.”

Sela’s expression changed. She reached for the child. “Put her down here.”

The girl’s lungs made a faint clicking sound. Eli would have recognized it. Sela had heard it every night during his worst months, before the mainland treatment had steadied him. She adjusted the child’s mask and called for a second portable cylinder.

The woman’s face crumpled. “You’ll help us?”

“We’ll help your daughter.”

“And me?”

“If you can carry water, you can help us.”

The woman looked toward the shelves of supplies, then removed her jeweled coat. Beneath it she wore a sleeveless dress and no shoes. “Tell me where.”

At the opposite end of the room, Dava the security officer woke and tried to sit up.

“Don’t move,” Sela said.

“I have to report—”

“You have a fractured cheek and a wound that needs closing.”

“People are taking the armory.”

“Then your report can wait until you can breathe.”

Dava gripped Sela’s wrist. “They’ll kill the officers.”

“Not in this room.” Sela freed her hand gently. “But if your officers come here shooting, they will kill patients. Use the mesh. Tell them this clinic is treating everyone. Tell them the reserve tanks are guarded by patients, workers, and witnesses. Tell them the first person who fires loses the room.”

Dava swallowed. “You think they’ll listen?”

“No,” Sela said. “I think someone will.”

Eli was awake on a cot beside the old laundry intake. His portable support unit gave a soft, regular hiss. The treatment card from Tilbury had been taped to the top of the machine, its instructions enlarged by three different hands.

“Ma,” he whispered.

Sela bent over him at once. “I’m here.”

“Ward Four has the children’s nebulizers.”

“I know.”

“No, the locked cabinet in Ward Four. The hospital inventory said they were moved to the central tower, but they weren’t. They’re behind the old linen chute.”

Sela touched his forehead. “How do you know?”

“Lio told me. He was there before they moved us. Also, Room Twelve has three working pulse monitors. Room Twelve is listed as empty, but it isn’t. There are two patients under the names from the trial forms.”

He paused, breathing shallowly. The effort made his eyes water.

“Eli, stop.”

“I’m not tired.”

“You are twelve.”

“I’m also right.”

Sela gave a broken laugh that became almost a sob. She kissed his hair. “You are right. You’re going to tell me one thing at a time.”

He reached for the mesh receiver. “Can I talk to the other patients?”

She hesitated. Then she placed it beside him.

Eli began sending names and locations. His voice was thin, but the network carried it. A patient in Ring Six confirmed the nebulizers. Someone in the old hospital annex said the pulse monitors were still there. A woman named Lio asked for a route to the open clinic and received three answers, two of them conflicting. Sela’s volunteers checked each one before choosing the safest.

In the upper gardens, generosity arrived with violence close behind.

The first report said residents had opened the glass doors and started distributing fruit, mineral salts, and seed cakes. The second said a group of men had sealed the west pantry and were beating anyone who tried to enter. The third said mainland refugees had reached the garden through an external maintenance bridge and were being driven back with electrified poles.

Tomas read the messages aloud from the Ministry gallery. His voice had gone flat with exhaustion.

“Do we divert a security team?” he asked.

“Which security team?” Mara said.

“The ones still answering.”

“Are they verified?”

“Two officers claim they are protecting the pantry.”

“Protecting it from whom?”

“Everyone.”

Mara looked at the workers around her. The platform crew had stopped pretending not to listen. Some had family in the upper gardens. Others had spent their lives being refused entry.

“Put out a call for unarmed witnesses,” she said. “Workers, medics, residents. Tell them to form a visible line between the pantry and the crowd. No one goes in carrying a weapon. Food distribution by count, not by tier. Record what is taken.”

“And if the officers fire?”

“Publish their names and move people away from the tanks.”

“That may not stop them.”

“No,” Mara said. “But it gives everyone else something to do besides panic.”

The call went out. In the minutes that followed, the mesh filled with the sounds of the city changing itself: doors forced open, arguments, crying children, shouted inventories, prayers, mechanical alarms. A group of gardeners used wheelbarrows to block an armored vehicle. A former transit inspector guided people around a collapsed stairwell. Two security officers laid down their weapons at a clinic entrance and began carrying stretchers.

Then the pantry guards fired.

The report arrived without image, only words: THREE INJURED. ONE TANK PUNCTURED. FIRE RISK.

Mara’s stomach tightened. “Tomas, tell them not to fight near the storage wall. The pantry vents into the oxygen distribution spine.”

“I’m sending it.”

Nia swore. “The pressure just dropped on our side.”

Mara turned toward the junction. “Can you isolate the line?”

“Maybe. If the old service gate still responds.”

“Do it only with a second reading.”

Nia gave her a hard look. “I know.”

“I’m saying it for everyone listening.”

The mainland engineer at the far end of the platform lifted a handheld gauge. “Independent pressure loss confirmed. Two-point decline.”

Nia moved. Workers followed her without being ordered. They crawled through the emergency passage Mara had found, carrying braces and a manual crank. The passage smelled of hot metal and wet stone. Behind them, Tomas broadcast the danger and the retreat condition: if the oxygen spine reached the second threshold, all nonessential teams were to withdraw.

Mara stayed on the mesh, directing people away from the failing route. She heard Sela tell the pantry crowd to extinguish open flames. She heard Dava, the wounded officer, identify the guards by name and order them to lower their weapons. She heard someone on Garden Seven say that the refugees could enter through the eastern glasshouse.

Not everyone listened. A man shouted that mainlanders had come to steal the city. Another answered that the city had been stealing the mainland for generations. The argument became a scuffle. A child began screaming.

Mara cut into the channel.

“Stop. The garden’s eastern glasshouse is open. There is food in the north store, but the north store is not a shelter. The shelter is beneath the seed archive. If you are carrying someone who cannot walk, say so. If you have food, report it. If you are hoarding food, understand that a locked pantry is not security when the air system depends on shared access.”

Her voice shook. She let it.

“I am afraid too. I do not know whether every relay will answer. I do not know how many shelters will remain safe. I know that destroying food, filters, or one another will make the descent worse. Open the doors you can open. Stand beside the doors you cannot. Make a record.”

For a moment, the channel quieted.

Then a young voice said, “Garden Seven eastern glasshouse open. Twenty-three refugees inside. We have tomatoes and two injured people.”

Another voice followed. “Ring Three pantry unlocked. We are counting.”

“Shelter Twelve has space for forty.”

“Upper lift sealed by officers. We are cutting the lock.”

At the west platform, Nia’s team reported the service gate isolated. The pressure decline slowed, then stopped.

“Not safe,” Nia said over the mesh. “But not worsening.”

Mara exhaled.

Above them, Lumen descended through the bruised clouds. The city’s old advertisements still flickered on distant towers, offering advancement, purity, security. Their colors bled across the storm like dying stars. Below, through breaks in the cloud, Mara saw the dark geometry of the mainland and tiny points of moving light: evacuation convoys, clinics, boats, relay stations answering one another.

The social order had not ended cleanly. It was breaking in rooms, at doors, beside locked cabinets and damaged engines. Some people opened what they had. Some held knives over it. Some stood between them and counted.

Tomas’s voice returned, hoarse but steady. “Mara, central chamber requests a status from the west platforms.”

She looked at Nia, at the mixed-tier crew crouched around the isolated gate, at the map beneath her hand marked with routes that had once been forbidden.

“West platform is holding,” she said. “The route remains open. We have not repaired the engine.”

She waited for the next tremor.

“Tell central to record that exactly.”

The city shuddered again. Across the mesh, doors continued to open.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Former Lumen apprentice cartographer, currently on Lumen’s exposed west outer platforms with Nia and the mixed-tier Junction H repair team after leaving the central control console under distributed oversight. She is exhausted, frightened, and in pain from her reopened shoulder and bruised leg, with toxic condensate exposure nearby, but remains focused on guiding teams through disputed routes, preserving local knowledge, and keeping civilians alive during the descent. She used her old bureaucratic maps and hidden pencil routes to identify an emergency crawlway, helped the team isolate a worsening pressure loss through independent readings, and broadcast witness-verified instructions to open gardens and shelters, share oxygen, remove citizenship restrictions, preserve life-support systems, and report uncertainty. She knows Tomas’s father released the emergency channels and was shot, that the mainland relay coordinates and restricted records are public, that mainland relays are beginning conversion, Junction H is taking load but is not fully repaired, and Lumen is descending irregularly. She carries her waterproof route map, notebook, drafting tools, collaborative relay maps, public witness-verified survival ledger, recorder with hospital and Council evidence, grease pencil, forged maintenance identification, black file on Darian Venn’s murder, hospital data core, mainland treatment card, one of three Crown Seal keys, and the distributed command schedule. She remains bonded to Eli and Sela and partnered with Tomas, Imani, and Nia, while refusing sole authority.

set.name: Sela Venn
set.description: Mara and Eli’s mother, currently in Ring Eight’s open emergency clinics and filtration labor block, coordinating treatment of injured protesters, Council officers, and elite residents without status checks; oxygen reserves; patient identification by name; and movement toward safer shelters over the emergency mesh. She is exhausted, underfed, bruised, and marked by chemical burns but remains alert and steady. She knows Rusk’s confession and death, the mainland coordinates, and the relay conversion are public, that outer-platform repairs are underway, that Eli is stabilized and helping identify hospital resources, and that security violence, hoarding, refugee attacks, and infrastructure failures continue. Her immediate goals are to keep Ring Eight’s filters and clinics functioning, protect Eli and rescued patients, verify or challenge dangerous orders, and move vulnerable people toward safer shelters as Lumen descends. She remains deeply bonded to Mara and Eli and allied with Imani and the mainland network.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Twelve-year-old former respiratory trial candidate, currently awake but weak in Ring Eight’s emergency clinics under portable respiratory support and mainland treatment. His breathing is stabilized but shallow. He knows the city is falling, the emergency channels are open, Rusk’s official history has been exposed, and the conversion is being organized through distributed witnesses rather than a single command. From his cot he used the emergency mesh to identify hidden children’s nebulizers, working pulse monitors, and patients concealed by obsolete trial records, helping Sela and other caregivers locate resources. He may continue communicating patient needs, but his immediate needs remain uninterrupted oxygen, monitoring, further treatment, and protection from renewed experimentation. He remains deeply bonded to Mara and Sela and surrounded by caregivers who identify patients by name rather than value.

set.name: Tomas Rusk
set.description: Junior communications aide and Minister Rusk’s son, currently in the Broadcast Ministry emergency gallery, continuing the emergency mesh after security officers shot his father during the open confession. He is exhausted, grieving, physically bruised with painful ribs and a swollen face, and emotionally shaken, but has published the shooting and responsible officers’ names and continues coordinating without turning his father’s death into vengeance. He holds the active authorization pattern and coordinates channels through local verification, two-station confirmation, published uncertainty, and rotating control rather than central command. He knows Junction H is holding after a locally verified repair, the west platform pressure loss has been isolated, mainland relays are beginning the corresponding sequence, several stations remain uncertain or silent, and low-lying communities are evacuating while Lumen’s residents divide between cooperation, hoarding, and violence. He carries the forged access slate, emergency protocol R-17, Ministry authorization patterns, relay knowledge, hospital transfer data, copied black-file access information, and one of three Crown Seal keys. His immediate goals are to keep the emergency mesh operating, transmit verified conditions and failures, protect civilians and infrastructure, and connect outer-platform and mainland teams. He remains intimately bonded to Mara, respects Imani and Nia’s judgment, and rejects vengeance.

set.name: Imani Okafor
set.description: Former Lumen atmospheric engineer, currently in the central control chamber with technicians and relay operators, monitoring the open-regulator conversion under distributed oversight. She is physically tired and vigilant, carrying portable medical gear, relay materials, and technical knowledge of pressure gates, filtration, atmospheric medicine, relay timing, and controlled conversion. She knows Rusk confessed publicly and was shot, Tomas is maintaining the emergency mesh, mainland coordinates and records are public under local verification rules, Junction H has begun taking load, the west platform pressure loss was isolated rather than solved, and multiple mainland relays are answering with uncertainty. She conditionally trusts Mara and Tomas, respects Nia’s practical skill, and remains committed to distributed repair.
